Wernicke's area was thought to be mostly linked to understanding speech. A landmark new study has something more to say.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new study has rewritten the role of one of the brain's major speech hubs, opening new possibilities for treating people who can't communicate verbally due to brain damage.

The study, published Thursday (Nov. 19) in the journal Science, may help to solve a 150-year-old mystery in neuroscience.

Nowadays, neuroscientists use cutting-edge tools to tease apart the junctions and wiring of our complex brains. But some basic theories in the field are far from new and rest on past discoveries. One of those theories concerns how the brain produces and comprehends speech.

In the 1860s, German neuroanatomist Carl Wernicke identified an area of the brain that is critical to speech and usually found in the temporal lobe on the left side of the organ. Damage to Wernicke's area makes it challenging for people to understand what others are saying ‪—‬ a condition known as Wernicke's aphasia. Therefore, the brain region has been primarily thought of as a decoder that helps us break down the meaning of other people's speech.

Wernicke's area (red) is found in the left temporal lobe.

But that isn't the whole story. While people who have Wernicke's aphasia can speak in a normal cadence, the words they use don't match their intention. They might substitute semantically related words, with "shoe" becoming "foot," or they might mix up words that have similar sounds, like "leg" and "peg." This can make their sentences sound like nonsensical word salad and thus undermine patients' ability to communicate.

These symptoms make it clear that damage to Wernicke's area affects not just speech comprehension but also speech production. But neuroscientists couldn't identify how this function arose in the brain region or which cells contributed to it.

The question "has remained a mystery for over 150 years now," said study co-author Alexander Silva, a neuroscientist at the University of California, San Francisco.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"One hypothesis is [that] it acts kind of like a proofreader. It listens to you speak, and it corrects errors," Silva explained. "But another is that there's actually dedicated activity in this area that generates upcoming speech."

In their new study, Silva and his colleagues set out to solve the conundrum, using a series of complementary tests that involved recording people's brain activity as they spoke. They had access to powerful tools for understanding brain function, like electrocorticography electrodes, which are implanted onto the brain's surface to measure neural activity. The precision of these tools enabled the team to investigate Wernicke's area at high temporal and spatial resolutions, Silva told Live Science.

The team recruited 28 participants with epilepsy, who already had electrodes implanted to monitor their seizures. They identified a small group of brain cells within Wernicke's area that fired about a quarter of a second before participants spoke words aloud. The signal seemed to be preparing for the speech production, and it could be separated from linked auditory signals made by cells responding to the resulting sound of the spoken words.

But this evidence alone couldn't prove that these cells actually caused speech; it could only correlate the signal with speech production. To connect the dots, the scientists mapped the brains of hundreds of people who were undergoing surgery to have temporal-lobe tumors removed and tested how the surgery affected their speech.

This analysis supported their previous findings; patients were much more likely to have trouble speaking after surgery if the procedure had damaged Wernicke's area, suggesting the area had a role in speech production.

We already knew that damage to Wernicke's area can lead to speech production errors, but this publication answers why.

Finally, in 13 people with implanted electrodes and undamaged Wernicke's areas, the researchers tested what happened when they stimulated the brain. When the scientists sent a wave of electricity through the speech-preparation area just before participants opened their mouths to talk, the stimulation caused them to make word errors that resembled Wernicke's aphasia.

The researchers then moved on to a different question: Could these discoveries about Wernicke's area help people whose speech is affected by brain damage?

Using more electrode data, the team identified individual brain cells in Wernicke's area that were linked to saying particular words. Then, they looked at two patients with speech paralysis; these individuals were unable to speak after strokes damaged their brainstems and they'd had electrodes implanted in their brains that sent signals to brain-computer speech devices.

The devices which interpret signals from undamaged areas of the brain to spell out words the patients are trying to say onto a screen. In these patients, the scientists monitored activity from neurons in Wernicke's area with electrodes and were able to decode what the participants were attempting to communicate.

Silva said these discoveries rewrite the textbook on Wernicke's area. Adeen Flinker, a neuroscientist at New York University who was not involved in the study, agreed.

"We already knew that damage to Wernicke's area can lead to speech production errors, but this publication answers why," Flinker told Live Science.

The new findings could lead to better brain-computer interfaces for treating aphasia, Silva said. Until now, patients who have benefited from these interfaces have mainly had problems with the pathways linking their motor cortex and mouth muscles, he said, such as people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).

"This is actually a small number of patients relative to the number of patients that have aphasia ‪—‬ so a language disorder from injury to the cortex itself," Silva said. These patients have vocal paralysis but are unable to benefit from BCIs because of this cortical damage, Flinker noted.

This special spot in Wernicke's area could be a new target for brain-computer interfaces aimed at helping patients with aphasia, Silva continued. "We really think that this is an area that could expand the number of people that could benefit from the technology in the near future," he concluded.

#6346. Movement can change how quickly you learn from the same visual clues

In a virtual reality study, swinging a lightsaber or throwing a punch helped volunteers learn visual patterns that required combining two features.

In the textbook account, learning happens in the head, and the hands do nothing more than report the answer.

Volunteers learned to sort striped discs more accurately when they answered by swinging a virtual lightsaber or punching a virtual target.

The advantage appeared when they had to judge the angle and thickness of the stripes together.

In the punching experiment, volunteers kept their lead when they switched to button presses immediately after training.

For sorting tasks that could be solved with explicit rules, bigger movements gave volunteers no clear advantage.

Luke Rosedahl is an assistant professor of biomedical engineering in Florida Atlantic University‘s College of Engineering and Computer Science.

Professor Rosedahl conducted the experiments at Brown University with Yuka Sasaki and Takeo Watanabe.

The 160 participants were young adults recruited around Brown, sorting striped discs in a headset, so how far the result reaches outside a lab is still open.

“We found that larger movements substantially improved learning when people had to recognize patterns by integrating multiple features, but provided no meaningful benefit when people learned categories using explicit rules,” Rosedahl said.

“Even more intriguing, the benefit occurred whether participants swung at the target or punched a separate response box. The movement itself appeared to matter, not whether it directly interacted with what they were learning.”

Some categories come with a rule. If it has whiskers and meows, it’s a cat. Psychologists call these rule-based categories, and people learn them by testing hypotheses, which is thought to lean on the front of the brain.

Other categories can’t be put into words. A radiologist’s sense that a lesion looks aggressive comes from weighing several features at once, and so does a driver’s read on whether a road is icy.

People learn these by comparing each new case with ones they’ve seen.

That kind of learning is thought to run through the striatum, a deep brain structure tied to movement and habits.

Both kinds were tested with the same material: gray discs striped at different angles and thicknesses, shown one at a time in a virtual reality hallway.

For the rule-based version, thickness and angle could be judged separately. For the other version, the dividing line ran diagonally through both, so no single feature gave the answer.

In the first experiment, 80 people each sorted 600 discs into two groups over 12 blocks, with the disc flashing green or red after every answer. Half answered by pulling a controller trigger.

The other half swung a virtual lightsaber and hit the disc.

On the hard, no-rule categories, the swingers pulled ahead by the second block and stayed ahead for most of the session.

On the rule-based categories, the swingers did very slightly worse, by an amount that could have been chance.

A swing takes longer than a button press, and it touches the thing being judged. Either could have been the real cause.

In a second experiment with 80 new volunteers, some punched a virtual response box separate from the disc, while others pulled a controller trigger.

Every disc stayed on screen for 2.5 seconds, however quickly they answered.

The rule-based task was also made harder, with two rules to discover instead of one, in case the first version had simply been too easy to show a difference.

Punching still helped on the no-rule categories and still did nothing for the rule-based ones. Slower answers went with worse accuracy, not better, so taking extra time wasn’t the reason.

In the final 100 training trials of the task that required combining both features, volunteers who punched got 90.7% of answers right, compared with 81.0% for those who pressed a button.

Then everyone switched. The punchers moved to buttons and scored 89.5%, almost unchanged. The button group moved to punching and scored 83.1%.

Whatever the big movements had built was still there when the movement stopped, which points to better learning rather than a boost at the moment of answering.

The authors can’t say what the arm is doing for the brain, and they said so. They offered two possibilities.

One possibility is that more effortful movements increase dopamine release in the striatum, which could help reinforce learning.

Effortful actions have also been shown to steer attention toward the features that matter. And movement has helped in other corners of learning, the authors wrote, such as writing by hand to learn to recognize letters.

The selectivity is the clue. If swinging had simply made people more engaged, Rosedahl’s team wrote, both kinds of categories should have improved.

The benefit appeared only when people had to combine visual features, a kind of learning thought to involve motor circuits.

The result also raises a question about decades of earlier work, nearly all of it done with button presses.

Those studies found that no-rule categories are learned slowly and that written instructions on how to perform them don’t help.

The authors suggested that the buttons themselves may have been holding that learning back.

The team didn’t record which hand participants favored, and controllers were handed out in no particular order, so the role of handedness and motor experience is unmeasured.

Other category types, such as rules with exceptions, may respond differently. And everything happened with participants seated and a headset on.

The team wrote that the next studies should test the effect in real training, in fields such as radiology and aviation.

There, the judgments that can’t be put into words are the ones that take years to learn. Rosedahl framed the stakes in one line.

“Incorporating movement could offer a simple way to improve learning in situations where conventional approaches fall short,” he said.

Whether a bigger swing of the arm can speed up a radiologist’s eye, and not only a student’s sorting of striped discs, is the test that comes next.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6345. Trump says no Iran deal needed after conflict drove GOP’s midterm losses

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance salute during a Wednesday ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery in honor of Veterans Day. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

President Donald Trump on Thursday shut down his administration’s on-again-off-again talks with Iran, saying he would not seek a deal to formally end the nine-month-old conflict with Tehran.

The possible end of the pursuit of a diplomatic solution came nine days after Trump and congressional Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections. House Democrats will have more than 250 seats come January, and Senate Democrats will have at least 55 seats in the Senate — with Alaska’s competitive race still uncalled.

Polls leading up to Election Day and since have shown that a majority of voters, and a sizeable chunk of Trump’s Republican base, felt the Iran conflict was a mistake.

Vice President JD Vance penned a lengthy social media post the day after the election, blaming, in large part, the Iran war for the coast-to-coast Democratic victories. Some GOP lawmakers have also called for an end to the conflict, which drove up fuel and other commodity prices.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote the morning after the GOP wipeout. "The president himself said so last night."

Trump has said that he agrees with Vance’s assessment but that if he had to decide again whether to join Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in striking Iranian targets, he would reach the same conclusion. On Monday, he told reporters that the Iran war "militarily is effectively over."

Vance had been Trump’s designated top negotiator in the talks with Iran’s remaining leaders, but the president said Thursday on social media that he had ordered his second-in-command to instead “focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.”

“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” he added. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!"

The situation along the Strait of Hormuz remains contested and dangerous for commercial vessels, including ones that deliver a large amount of the world’s oil products. Iranian officials contend that they control most of the key waterway.

Trump, Vance and other administration officials have said in recent weeks that they were open to continuing talks with Iran, while criticizing Tehran's negotiating tactics. Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also is Trump’s national security adviser, told reporters that Iran's latest demands were unreasonable.

Trump’s announcement Thursday could represent his latest way to try assuaging GOP voters, including members of his “Make America Great Again” base. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted after the midterms and released Tuesday showed that a majority of Republicans (51 percent) want Congress to pass legislation that would end the Iran conflict. Overall, 71 percent of Americans would support such a bill, the survey found.

The conflict was front-and-center during the midterms campaign.

Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, who lost the Senate race in Michigan to Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, called for the Iran conflict to end "quickly."

“Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life. Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down," Rogers said in one campaign ad.

On Capitol Hill, GOP lawmakers have tried giving Trump cover, while raising some concerns about high gas prices and questioning whether the president and his team have a viable exit strategy.

As the midterms campaign hit the homestretch in late September, two Iowa Republicans in tight races, Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, voted with Democrats on a measure to end the conflict.

“With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” Nunn, an Air Force veteran, wrote on social media. “I will not support another open-ended war.”

Nunn and Miller-Meeks both lost their seats last week, despite breaking with the president over the war.

Trump’s declaration this week of a military end to the Iran war came more than seven years after he offered some foreshadowing during a June 25, 2019, exchange with this CQ Roll Call reporter in the Oval Office.

Asked that day what his exit strategy would be if war ever broke out with Iran, he said: “You’re not going to need an exit strategy. I don’t do exit strategies.”

#6344. Prickly pear cacti generate electricity, and sunlight changes their voltage

Prickly pear cacti generate a small voltage that varies with sunlight, and researchers are exploring whether it could power field sensors.

In a California greenhouse, a row of prickly pear cacti is quietly generating electricity. A single stem can produce about half a volt.

When eight stems were wired together, they reached 4.5 volts, three times the voltage of a standard AA battery.

The trick depends on the unusual way cacti photosynthesize. They store up acid overnight and use it up in daylight.

That turns each stem into something like a small living solar panel.

The work was led by the University of California, Santa Cruz (UCSC).

Most plants take in carbon dioxide during the day. They open tiny pores in their leaves, let the gas in and use sunlight to turn it into sugar.

The downside is that water escapes through those open pores. In a desert, that’s a costly trade.

Prickly pears and some of their relatives work around this problem. Aloe, pineapple, and dragon fruit use a system called crassulacean acid metabolism, or CAM for short.

These plants keep their pores closed in the heat of the day and open them in the cool of the night. They pull in carbon dioxide while it’s dark and store it as malic acid, the same acid that makes green apples sour.

When the sun comes up, they break the acid down and finish making sugar.

The cactus’s shape provides the second part of the trick. Prickly pear stems are thick and opaque, another way of holding on to water, so photosynthesis happens only in the outer two millimeters or so.

When morning light hits one side of a stem, that side starts using up its stored acid. The shaded side keeps its acid.

The result is a difference in acidity across the stem, from one face to the other. That difference creates a voltage, and the researchers tap into it with a wired electrode inserted into the plant.

In effect, the cactus charges overnight and releases the energy during the day.

The idea came from Michael Loik, a professor of environmental studies who has studied cactus physiology and ecology for about 40 years.

“I’ve been obsessed with the plant since forever, it seems,” Loik said.

He suspected the cacti could produce electricity. He and Charlie Chesney, then a PhD student in environmental studies, set out to prove it and measure it.

They used cacti in field plots at the UCSC Farm, in greenhouses, and in the lab. Chesney recruited a large group of undergraduates from engineering, the sciences, and the social sciences, and seven of them are now authors on the paper.

“The undergraduate students told me they liked this project so much because it felt whimsical, and like a light-hearted approach to something that is so serious,” said Chesney, who led the project.

“It was a fun way to explore climate solutions that put creativity first.”

When researchers wired eight stems together, they measured 4.5 volts, three times the nominal voltage of a standard AA battery.

The researchers are exploring whether prickly pears could power low-energy field sensors. The voltage may also help growers monitor how the plants respond to changing conditions.

Chesney has since graduated. Colleen Josephson, an assistant professor of electrical and computer engineering, is continuing the work with her PhD student John Madden, and they are looking for ways to strengthen the signal.

The team also wanted to know how weather and growing conditions affect the voltage. The cacti behaved very much like solar panels.

Voltage was much higher in summer than in winter, and through the day it tracked the amount of sunlight.

“Just how closely the voltage aligned with the sunlight conditions was really surprising,” Chesney said.

“Comparing winter to summer voltage, the voltage really follows the same pattern of the amount of sunlight throughout the day.”

There is an upper limit. Too much sunlight and the cactus goes into self-protection mode.

“If it’s too high, then the cactus will start trying to protect itself from a sunburn, which will also decrease the voltage,” Chesney said. “There’s a balance, a mid-range of light that causes the voltage to be higher.”

Then came the drought test. The team stopped watering some cacti for 15 months.

The plants survived and kept photosynthesizing. Sometimes, they even produced more voltage than cacti that had been watered normally.

“This was a really surprising result, but also showed how resilient a cactus is – it could still produce electricity even when it seems, to us, like it’s near death,” Chesney said.

A separate experiment led by undergraduate Erin Langness looked at nitrogen, a common fertilizer ingredient.

Nitrogen increased the cacti’s store of malic acid, so they kept photosynthesizing and producing voltage later into the day.

The team isn’t trying to run homes on cacti. They have something smaller in mind.

The researchers are exploring whether prickly pears could power low-energy field sensors.

As climate change puts more pressure on crops, farmers increasingly use low-power sensors to monitor their fields.

The voltage may also help growers monitor how the plants respond to changing conditions.

That could be useful on farms that grow prickly pears for their edible pads, called nopales, and their fruit, called tunas.

“There are many commercial applications of cacti where monitoring their health using a low-power system like ours, that is just operating off on the side and is self-powered,” Loik said.

“This could be a really interesting avenue to pursue. It could be connected to a plant that acts as sentinel, measuring conditions and sending it back to the base station at the farmer’s office.”

Other CAM plants, such as agave and pineapple, might work too. The researchers note, however, that some of them may not tolerate the wires as well as the prickly pear does.

The study is published in the journal Plants, People, Planet.

#6342. A brain region known for listening helps us speak

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Recordings reveal how Wernicke’s area helps turn thoughts into words

A small bit of brain has big roles in understanding and producing speech, a new study finds.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

WASHINGTON — A part of the brain famous for listening is important for talking, too.

Data collected from people as they listen and try to talk show that this brain region, a small spot inside a larger area called Wernicke’s area, has a more expansive job than researchers thought when it comes to communicating. The results may help efforts to restore people’s voices. The results presented November 15 at the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience and published November 19 in Science.The study provides convincing evidence that this brain spot is critical for speech production, says neurologist and language researcher Jeffrey Binder of the Medical College of Wisconsin in Milwaukee. “My hope is that this study will help scientists and clinicians accept a more accurate interpretation of this focal area” as an early stop on the pathway to saying a word.

A small part of the brain, just above the left ear, was first described in 1874 by a neurologist Carl Wernicke as necessary for making sense of speech. People with damage there had trouble comprehending words. But some people also had trouble producing them. “Sounds were swapped, words were replaced with near misses,” Edward Chang of the University of California, San Francisco, said in a news briefing. “The basic question has been, ‘Why would damage to a hearing area of the brain break the ability to speak?’ That question has been open for 150 years.”The new research offers an answer: A small bit of Wernicke’s area (to be extremely specific, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus or lpSTG ) becomes active just before a word is spoken. “Every word that you have said today began in that small part above your left ear about a quarter of a second before you said it,” Chang said.

The finding adds to growing evidence that brain areas are more complex than people have appreciated, says neuroscientist Leigh Hochberg at Brown University in Providence, R.I. “I believe that one of the things we are going to learn over the next five, 10 years of this research, is that each part of the brain that, we were taught as a med student or a grad student, does this, probably does that and a whole lot more.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Scientists measured brain activity in 28 people before they had surgery for epilepsy or tumors. They were able to see that this brain region kicked on as a person listened to words, and also just before they attempted to speak. Cells there had preferences for certain sorts of words, long ones, for instance. “It’s more active when you’re about to say the word caterpillar than when you’re about to say the word cat,” said Matthew Leonard, a cognitive neuroscientist at UCSF.

Electrical stimulation to this small bit of brain also interfered with people’s ability to talk. “What we found was that stimulation, really only in this lpSTG area, disrupted this speech production when it was delivered just prior to speaking,” said UCSF bioengineer Alexander Silva.

Some efforts to make implanted devices that can help restore speech to people who no longer talk focus on the motor cortex, a part of the brain that controls the movements required for speech. This bit of Wernicke’s area offers an additional spot to consider, Silva said. “What if you could target a single brain region and gain access to the full spectrum of speech, from listening all the way up to speech production?”

Experimental brain implants in two volunteers with paralysis were able to detect both what they heard and what they were trying to say, the researchers report in the study.

The discovery may help scientists better understand situations that involve both hearing and speaking, such as speech or comprehension differences in people with autism, or how children first begin learning to talk, Chang said.

Laura Sanders is the neuroscience writer. She holds a Ph.D. in molecular biology from the University of Southern California.

#6341. Scientists may have found a way to track one of North America’s most elusive turtles

A tiny flatworm found in diamondback terrapins and the snails they eat may help scientists understand how turtle populations are connected.

Diamondback terrapins are hard to find and harder to count. A new study suggests that one of the best ways to follow them may be through a tiny flatworm that lives in their intestines and in the snails they eat.

By reading this parasite’s genes along the US Atlantic coast, scientists found that its populations split into distinct groups.

They also found a genetic dividing line about 300 kilometers south of where turtle experts had drawn the boundary between two terrapin subspecies.

The study was carried out by researchers from Florida Atlantic University’s Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute and East Carolina University.

The diamondback terrapin is the only North American turtle that lives exclusively in brackish water, in salt marshes and estuaries along the coast. For a long time, people mostly ate it.

Turtle soup was a fashionable dish, and hunting for it drove the species into steep decline until the early 20th century. Then, in 1920, Prohibition banned sherry, a key ingredient in most turtle soup recipes.

Demand collapsed, and so did the hunting.

That wasn’t a happy ending, though. Terrapins kept declining because of habitat loss, coastal development, and drowning in crab pots.

The species is now listed as “vulnerable” on the IUCN Red List. Conservationists want better data on where terrapin populations live and how they’re connected.

But the turtles are secretive and spread out, and catching enough to answer those questions is slow, expensive work.

The parasite is a fluke called Pleurogonius malaclemys. It can’t complete its life without two hosts.

Its eggs pass out in terrapin droppings and are eaten by eastern mudsnails. Inside the snail, the fluke multiplies by cloning itself.

Its larvae then leave the snail’s soft body and form small pearly cysts on the hard plate the snail uses to seal its shell.

When a terrapin eats an infected snail, the fluke grows into an adult in the turtle’s gut and reproduces sexually there.

This arrangement is what makes the fluke useful. Mudsnails are abundant and easy to collect, and they barely move.

Terrapins are the ones that carry the parasite from marsh to marsh. If the turtles don’t travel, the fluke’s genes don’t travel either. In principle, the parasite’s family tree should trace the turtle’s movements.

“One of the biggest challenges in conserving vulnerable species is understanding how populations are distributed and connected without having to capture and handle large numbers of animals,” said senior author Michael McCoy from FAU Harbor Branch.

“Our findings show that this parasite may provide an important window into the ecology of diamondback terrapins.”

The team collected mudsnails from Cape Cod in Massachusetts to St. Augustine in Florida and dissected more than 4,000 of them. Infections inside the snails were rare, never reaching 4% at any site.

The cysts outside were far more common, appearing on as many as 74% of snails at some marshes. Altogether, the fluke turned up at 23 of the 29 marshes sampled.

Finds on Cape Cod and in northeast Florida pushed its known range further north and south.

The Wetlands Institute provided the researchers with 38 female terrapins that had been killed by cars in New Jersey.

Seventeen of them carried adult flukes, with up to seven worms per turtle.

From 476 genetic sequences, the team found 102 distinct versions of a stretch of the fluke’s mitochondrial DNA. More than three-quarters of these versions turned up at only one location.

One version dominated the northern marshes, and another dominated the south. The farther apart two marshes were, the more their flukes differed genetically.

That fits what is known about terrapins. The most mobile of them, adult females, have been recorded traveling no more than 8.5 kilometers. If the hosts stay close to home, their parasites become local too.

The most striking result was where the sharpest split fell. Biologists have traditionally drawn the line between the northern diamondback terrapin and the Carolina terrapin at Cape Hatteras in North Carolina.

The fluke’s genetic break falls instead between Wilmington, North Carolina, and Charleston, South Carolina, near the state border. That’s about 300 kilometers further south.

Terrapin subspecies were originally defined by their appearance, before genetic tools existed, so the parasite’s data adds to growing questions about where the real boundaries lie.

The study also turned up something nobody had described before. Most fluke cysts are pearly white, but some had a faint blush or a pink ring around the edge, while others were bright fuchsia.

They first appeared in North Carolina in 2023 and later in Massachusetts and New Jersey, sometimes on the same snail as ordinary cysts. The color is in the cyst wall, not in the larva inside.

The pink cysts didn’t match any genetic group, and the researchers don’t yet know what causes them. One possibility is that they are simply older.

The authors make a broader point. Parasites account for nearly half of all known species, yet they are rarely studied and almost never protected.

When a host declines, its parasites decline with it. Scientists recently formed an IUCN group dedicated to parasite conservation, and this study adds basic range and diversity data for a parasite that has been almost entirely ignored.

The team is careful not to overstate the results. The analysis used a single genetic marker, which is inherited only through the mother.

No one has yet compared fluke genetics directly with terrapin genetics from the same marshes, and that test will decide whether the fluke truly mirrors its host.

Counting cysts is also not a straightforward way to count turtles. One earlier study found that cyst numbers explained less than 8% of the variation in terrapin abundance.

“Our results point to an opportunity to look at conservation from a different perspective,” McCoy said.

“Rather than relying exclusively on direct observations of terrapins, we can investigate the organisms that depend on them.”

“Understanding where these parasites occur and how their populations are genetically connected could help scientists identify important geographic divisions and develop better questions about how terrapin populations should be monitored and managed.”

The study is published in the journal Ecology and Evolution.

NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft just reached 1 light-day from our planet, but a newfound glitch in the probe's onboard computer is preventing it from sharing science data with Earth.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA has confirmed that its Voyager 1 spacecraft has reached a record-breaking 1 light-day from Earth — but new milestones come with old problems.

On Nov. 14, the Voyager mission team discovered that the nearly 50-year-old space probe had stopped sending science data back to Earth, according to NASA — a problem that the team had to deal with as recently as 2024. As of Thursday (Nov. 19), the team had not resolved the problem.

But they did detect a "carrier" signal that is used to ferry science and engineering information from Voyager 1 to Earth, confirming that the probe is still powered up and pointed in the right direction.

"We have an anomaly that is not unseen before," Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager, said at a NASA news conference Thursday, adding that she is "confident" that the science data will continue flowing again soon.

Using the carrier signal, the team confirmed that the probe had reached its latest distance milestone of 1 light-day from Earth, or roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) away, Wednesday (Nov. 18). At this distance, which no human-made object had ever reached before, it takes a full 24 hours for radio signals traveling at the speed of light to get from Earth to Voyager 1 and vice versa. (The spacecraft's twin probe, Voyager 2, is expected to reach its own light-day in 2035.)

This incredible distance, coupled with the spacecraft's five-decade-old hardware, makes troubleshooting problems on the probe extremely arduous, Dodd explained.

An illustration depicting Voyager 1 at one light-day from Earth.

"It takes two days to diagnose anything with the spacecraft — so we can't do anything fast, and the data rates are very low," she said. "We are in a realm where we're going to see more anomalies with Voyager, just due to the distance and the age."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

According to NASA, the current glitch likely stems from Voyager's onboard computer, which is responsible for collecting data from its science instruments and transmitting it back to Earth in a readable format. The team encountered a similar problem in November 2023 that prevented Voyager 1 from sharing science data until engineers solved the issue in June 2024. The mission team is approaching this new glitch the same way they solved the previous one, NASA wrote in a blog post.

If the fix succeeds, Voyager 1 will continue transmitting data from its two remaining science instruments — a magnetometer, which measures magnetic fields in interstellar space, and a plasma wave detector, which measures charged particles in the interstellar medium. To conserve power on the aging spacecraft, the mission team shut off some of Voyager's instruments earlier this year while powering other, more efficient ones in a "Big Bang" maneuver that should keep the probe alive through at least 2027.

We are in a realm where we're going to see more anomalies with Voyager, just due to the distance and the age

However, it's only a matter of time before Voyager 1 runs out of juice and closes its mechanical eyes to the cosmos. After that, it will continue drifting through interstellar space indefinitely, carrying a Golden Record of images, music and information about life on Earth. In the meantime, Voyager will continue learning everything it can about the strange environment of the interstellar medium — the space between stars, where only Voyagers 1 and 2 have ever been before.

Voyager 1 officially reached interstellar space in 2012, after transforming our views of Jupiter, Saturn and other solar system bodies. For more about the probe's incredible discoveries, check out our collection of Voyager 1's iconic photos.

#6339. In 1988, ice covered 1.66 square miles near the summit of Indonesia’s Puncak Jaya, and now what is left would fit on about a dozen soccer fields

Landsat images show the ice near the summit of Puncak Jaya in Indonesia has dwindled to small patches that no longer flow like glaciers.

In 1988, glaciers covered about 1.66 square miles (4.31 square kilometers) near the summit of Puncak Jaya, on the island of New Guinea. By September 2025, about 0.03 square miles (0.09 square kilometers) were left.

That’s roughly 2 percent. What’s left would fit on about a dozen soccer fields.

It also no longer moves. The patches are too thin and too broken up to behave like a glacier, NASA Earth Observatory reported on November 16.

Puncak Jaya stands in the Sudirman Range, in the Indonesian part of New Guinea. Very few places this close to the equator have held ice all year round.

Next door is the largest stretch of warm ocean water on the planet. So the glaciers here sit near the warmest conditions in which year-round ice can survive at all.

Scientists have called them high-altitude canaries in the coal mine. Other members of that small club are what’s left of Humboldt Glacier in Venezuela, the ice fields of Kilimanjaro in Tanzania and the Quelccaya Ice Cap in Peru, a country that has lost more than half of its glaciers in six decades.

NASA compared two false-color pictures of the range. Landsat 5 took one on November 3, 1988. Landsat 9 took the other on October 19, 2026.

Ice shows up light blue, bare rock brown, clouds white and plants green. In 1988, blue caps several of the highest ridges. In 2026 there are only a few small blue fragments, and brown rock covers most of the old icy ridgetops.

The area figures come from Donaldi Permana, a climate scientist at Indonesia’s Agency for Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics (BMKG). The 2025 number is based on satellite and aerial data.

An aerial survey is planned for December. It should show how much ice is left in 2026, Permana said.

The ice got thinner, too. At the main monitoring site, on the East Northwall Firn, it was 105 feet (32 meters) thick in 2010, Permana said.

In 2023 it measured 13 feet (4 meters). By November 2024 there was no ice there at all.

Thinning ice also cracks apart. Each new piece has fresh edges where it can melt, and so the losses feed on themselves.

In the 2026 image, newly bared rock sits between the remnants. Snow still falls on the mountain. It just doesn’t stay on the bare rock long enough to turn into new ice.

“It’s a house of cards problem,” said Chris Shuman, a retired University of Maryland glaciologist who has followed Puncak Jaya’s glaciers in satellite images. “Once this process gets going, there’s really no turning back.”

To count as a glacier, a body of ice generally has to do two things. It has to be thick enough to creep downhill under its own weight. And it needs a zone where snow piles up faster than it melts.

On Puncak Jaya, the ice is now so thin, and so split into small, stagnant patches, that it has stopped flowing.

“While small ice remnants persist in high-altitude crevices around Puncak Jaya, their functional life as active glaciers is effectively over,” Permana said.

El Niño years are especially rough on these glaciers. Warmer air pushes the freezing level above the summit, so rain falls instead of snow.

Fresh snow is white. It bounces sunlight away and protects the ice underneath. Without it, the darker surface soaks up heat and melts faster.

During the 2015-2016 El Niño, the ice thinned about five times faster than normal, a finding NASA links to a study in PNAS. In one year it lost roughly 17 feet (5.3 meters) of thickness.

Then came the 2023-2024 El Niño. The ice thinned again, by about 7 to 13 feet (2 to 4 meters) a year.

Recent satellite studies suggest the main ice areas could be gone completely around 2030. For this, NASA links a study published in The Cryosphere.

BMKG’s own estimates suggest the ice could disappear much sooner, Permana noted, with the current El Niño speeding things up. Either way, Puncak Jaya’s ice looks set to vanish well before Africa’s remaining glaciers, which may be gone by 2040.

NASA links the 2 percent figure to a World Meteorological Organization report, State of the Climate in the South-West Pacific 2025.

The information was obtained from NASA Earth Observatory.

These lightweight, easy-to-store models get the job done with multiple attachments and powerful motors.

During testing, we found that being able to switch from cordless to handheld made it easier to transition from tackling small messes to deeper cleaning sessions.

Not every cordless stick vacuum we test ends up in this roundup. However, these other models still perform well and are reliable recommendations:

Dyson Gen5Detect Cordless Stick Vacuum: This cordless stick vacuum certainly commands a premium price, and you get a lot of the same features as the Dyson V15 Detect we recommend above, such as an LCD display screen, the Fluffy Optic cleaner head, and pet hair attachments. If you’re an allergy sufferer, you may prefer the Gen5Detect because its filtration system captures particles down to 0.1 microns, while the V15 filters down to just 0.3 microns. Plus, runtime is slightly longer on the Gen5Detect.

The main advantages of owning a cordless stick vacuum are easy portability and storage. But what you trade for the convenience is battery life and runtime. Most models clean from 30 to 60 minutes, but that’s also dependent on what setting you’re using. If you’re running the vacuum on its highest speed the entire time, it might die faster. Be wary of manufacturers’ advertised total runtime because it may represent performance on the lowest setting or using two fully charged batteries, for instance. Battery charging should also be factored in, so plan your cleaning session accordingly so you don’t lose power in the middle of a floor swipe.

Like we mentioned earlier, the dustbins on cordless stick vacuums are significantly smaller than those of an upright or canister unit. You should consider your cleaning habits and the spaces you usually vacuum to find a model that aligns with your needs. If you live in an apartment or are using the cordless vac to supplement your other cleaning supplies, then a dustbin with at least half a liter capacity should do. Some of the models we recommend hold up to one liter of debris, which helps limit the number of trips to the trash can.

Although not a necessity, having a good amount of attachments with your vacuum is especially helpful for cleaning hard-to-reach places or targeting specific issues. Crevice tools pick up dirt and dander from corners and couch cushions, while bristled brushes and motorized pet tools agitate and lift hair and fur that’s been embedded into upholstery.

A good filtration system helps combat allergens such as dust and pet dander that are being kicked up by a vacuum. The best option is a HEPA filter, or “high-efficiency particulate air” filter, which traps 99.97 percent of particles that are 0.3 microns or larger in size. A fully sealed or multi-step filtration system also has the potential to trap a wide variety of airborne allergens without releasing them back into your home.

Cordless vacuums are very effective at picking up pet hair, especially models designed with high suction power and specialized brush rolls. Some of the models we recommend include motorized attachments that lift embedded hair from upholstery and carpets. Anti-tangle vacuum heads are also a key feature that helps prevent hair from wrapping around the brush roll. While not all models perform equally, a high-quality cordless stick vacuum is able to handle pet hair just as well as traditional versions.

The lifespan of these vacuums typically lasts from three to five years, depending on usage, build quality, and maintenance. Battery performance plays a major role, since lithium-ion batteries start to lose capacity over time.

Avoiding overcharging and storing the vacuum properly could help extend the battery life significantly. Running regular maintenance like cleaning the vacuum filters and emptying the dustbin completely preserves suction and functionality. Higher-end models often last longer due to better materials and replaceable parts, but either price point has potential to last for years with proper care.

Modern designs are increasingly more effective at cleaning many surface types, including rugs and carpets. Advances in battery tech and general efficiency have allowed for strong suction performance that is comparable to corded models. Adjustable power modes allow for deeper cleaning on thicker carpets, and multi-roller and motorized brush heads agitate fibers to loosen dirt and debris.

Performance may vary depending on the type of flooring. Some vacuums are designed to work on low-to-medium pile carpets, while others are able to handle high-pile. It’s best to consult the listed features and specs of the model you’re considering to ensure it aligns with the flooring types in your home.

#6337. Solo meerkats can find their way back home

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Meerkats live, forage and raise their young in large groups. But they’ve still got solo skills

To test meerkats’ solo navigating skills, researchers outfitted the animals with GPS trackers, separated them from their packs, and followed their journeys back home.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

It was a hot, dry day in the Kalahari Desert, and Mathilde Martin was running after a meerkat.

The animal wore a GPS tracker around its neck and bolted between shelters, like an action hero running for cover, says Martin, a biologist at the University of Zurich. She and her colleagues had captured the meerkat earlier that morning, driven it 1.5 kilometers from its pack and then released it into the desert. They were trying to find out how well individual meerkats could find their way back home.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The answer was quite well, the researchers reported November 19 in the Journal of Experimental Biology. The results suggest that meerkats can navigate expertly on their own, perhaps relying on mental maps charted early in life. “They all seem to be very, very good,” Martin says. It’s a surprise finding for a species known for its group cooperation.

Meerkats (Suricata suricatta), which live in southern Africa, form tight-knit family groups of up to 50 members. These social animals cooperate in many aspects of life, including by babysitting each other’s pups and watching for predators while traveling along foraging paths. Martin and her colleagues thought meerkats might also rely on one another for navigating. Some pack members, perhaps those who’ve had more opportunity to explore solo, might have spatial knowledge of their territory and lead the rest, she says. But that’s not what the team discovered.

In separate catch and release experiments with 20 individual meerkats, 18 made a beeline back home, back to their group or back to the site where they were captured. (The other two may have been too stressed to get moving, Martin says.)

Neither age nor individual experience, which researchers had been tracking, seemed to factor into the meerkats’ homing skills. Nearly all of them knew where to go, Martin says. She thinks these crackerjack navigators relied on visual cues to orient themselves. They’d pop up on their hind legs and scan the landscape before scampering off in a direct line to their target.

It’s likely that scent played a role, too, though distant scent marks may have faded by the time the meerkats were released. The researchers dropped the animals off in territory they hadn’t visited for at least 30 days. “Otherwise,” she says, “it would have been a bit too easy for them to find their way back,” she says.

#6336. Swordfish hunt about 2,000 feet down, but every so often one plunges as deep as a mile, and scientists suspect it is reading the ocean

Satellite tags on 34 North Atlantic swordfish caught rare dives past 3,280 feet. They were short and came near eddies and fronts, hinting the fish check the ocean.

Swordfish spend their days hunting in the dark, about 2,000 feet (600 meters) below the surface. Every so often, one keeps going.

Satellite tags on North Atlantic swordfish have caught these rare plunges past 3,280 feet (1,000 meters). Nobody knows why the fish make them.

A team from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) has now looked at years of tagging data in search of an answer. The dives were short, fairly steady, and most common where surface temperatures varied and the sea surface stood higher. The authors think the fish may be sampling the water column, possibly to help them find their way. The study was published in Marine Biology.

Swordfish live in open oceans around the world, from about 45 degrees north to 45 degrees south. They follow a daily rhythm. By day they stay deep, usually between about 1,300 and 2,300 feet (400 and 700 meters), and at night they rise toward the surface.

That routine follows their food. Huge numbers of small animals live in the ocean’s twilight zone and move up and down each day, and swordfish track them. Like other large predators of the open sea, tuna and swordfish get much of their food from that dim layer.

Swordfish can handle water from about 36 to 88 degrees Fahrenheit (2 to 31 degrees Celsius). They keep their eyes and parts of their body warmer than the surrounding water, which helps them stay deep for long periods.

The researchers combined data from 34 pop-up satellite tags placed on North Atlantic swordfish between 2003 and 2024. Twenty-three were tagged off the Atlantic coast of Florida, six near the Grand Banks off Canada, three in the southern Sargasso Sea and two in the Gulf of America, also known as the Gulf of Mexico. Twenty-four were probably adults and 10 were probably juveniles.

The tags stayed on for one to six months and logged depth, temperature and light. Together, they covered 3,666 days of swordfish life.

The data came from a partnership with NOAA’s Southeast Fisheries Science Center and the Massachusetts Division of Marine Fisheries.

“It wouldn’t have been possible to analyze this from just a single tagging operation, or from a single lab,” said Simon Thorrold, a fish ecologist at WHOI and an author of the study.

The team flagged 39 days on which a fish went unusually deep for its own normal pattern. On 25 of those days, recorded by 10 tags, the data were detailed enough to confirm a distinct extreme dive.

These dives averaged about 3,250 feet (991 meters) at their deepest point, and the deepest reached roughly 5,460 feet (1,664 meters), more than a mile down. On ordinary days, the fish’s deepest point averaged about 2,090 feet (637 meters).

A single extreme dive lasted about 45 to 55 minutes on average. When a fish made one such dive in a day, it usually dropped two to three times faster than it climbed back. In one fish’s full-resolution record, it spent between a few seconds and about six minutes at the bottom.

The water at the bottom of these dives averaged about 47 degrees Fahrenheit (8.4 degrees Celsius). On other days, the coldest water the fish met averaged about 54 degrees Fahrenheit (12.1 degrees Celsius).

Most dives started and ended in the twilight zone, during daylight. In 12 of 16 such dives, the fish came back to within about 33 feet (10 meters) of the depth where it began.

The authors weighed seven possible reasons for deep dives, including feeding, escaping predators, saving energy and navigation.

Feeding seemed unlikely. A hunting fish would be expected to linger at depth, but these fish barely paused at the bottom before heading back up. The dives also did not cluster at dawn and dusk, when prey is easiest to reach.

Escape did not fit well either. The descents were steady, about 3.3 feet (1 meter) per second, and the fish behaved normally afterward. Only one dive began and ended near the surface at night, when the authors think predators may be more likely to be around. The authors could not rule out that the two juveniles, which made several dives in a single day, were avoiding predators.

Extreme dives were much more likely where sea surface temperature varied a lot and where the sea surface stood higher. In the team’s model, each extra degree Celsius of temperature variation made a dive about 23 times more likely. These conditions mark swirling eddies, fronts and major currents such as the Gulf Stream.

The authors suggest that crossing into a new water mass may prompt a swordfish to check what lies below. Short, repeatable dives of the same shape would fit that kind of sampling.

“They could be coming into an ocean weather system, like an eddy or a frontal system, where we have a change in water masses,” said Ciara Willis, who led the study as a doctoral student in the MIT-WHOI Joint Program and now works at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute.

Deeper water could also give a clearer reading of Earth’s magnetic field, which many fish can sense, away from the busy, changing layers near the surface. Some dives happened near seamounts, ridges and magnetic anomalies, but those links were weak, though rough seafloor showed a smaller but significant effect. Other ocean travelers are under similar suspicion, as oceanic manta rays also dive deep, apparently not to feed.

The authors stress that their conclusions are inferences. Satellite tag positions carry an average error of about 60 to 90 miles (100 to 150 kilometers), and possibly more for deep divers like swordfish. That makes it hard to match a dive to a specific seafloor feature.

It is still unclear how common these dives are among swordfish, and whether they differ between populations or ages.

Swordfish support valuable fisheries, so knowing what steers them could help predict where they go as the ocean changes.

The information was obtained from the study published in Marine Biology and from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution.

#6335. Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage declared winner of open House seat

Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, fifth from right, joins incoming members Thursday for their freshman class photo on the House steps outside the Capitol. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Paul LePage, the former Maine governor who once said he was “Donald Trump before Donald Trump,” is heading to Congress.

The Associated Press called the race for the open 2nd District on Thursday after the Maine Secretary of State’s office tabulated the votes under the state’s ranked choice voting system. LePage ended up ahead of Democratic state Auditor Matt Dunlap 50.8 percent to 49.2 percent.

Dunlap had already conceded the race to LePage, who will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden in the sprawling district, which includes much of Maine outside the Portland and Augusta areas.

“Paul LePage is already hard at work for the people of Maine attending Congressional orientation, meeting with national leaders, and making it clear the political parties need to work together for the American people,” Brent Littlefield, a senior adviser to LePage, said in a statement Thursday. “As Paul said, he will work with anyone, regardless of Party, to put Maine first.”

LePage’s win is a glimmer of good news for Republicans, who saw massive losses across the country in last week’s midterm elections. He is one of three Republicans, along with Texas’ Jace Yarbrough and Tennessee’s Brent Taylor, to have flipped a House seat, although Maine’s 2nd District is the only one of the three that wasn’t redrawn to favor the GOP.

LePage’s win also means that at least one Republican will continue to represent New England in Congress, taking up the mantle from Maine Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her own reelection bid last week.

Golden, who was first elected in 2018, had been a top Republican target throughout his time in Congress. But the lawmaker, known for bucking his party, proved difficult to unseat in the past two election cycles.

“I also know a thing or two about winning in tough circumstances. So, I know you have to tip your hat to Paul LePage for winning in the midst of this Blue Tsunami,” Golden said in a social media post last week.

Dunlap initially launched his campaign as a primary challenge to Golden in the fall of 2025, only for the congressman to announce his retirement a month later. Dunlap went on to win a four-way contest for the Democratic nomination.

#6334. A metal detectorist found a Viking sword and rare oval brooches on the Isle of Man, and his father had helped find the island’s only other pair

Daniel Crowe found a Viking sword, oval brooches and trading weights over 1,100 years old on the Isle of Man. His father helped find the island's only other pair.

A metal detectorist on the Isle of Man has found a Viking sword, a set of bronze brooches and trading weights and scales, all more than 1,100 years old. The objects are believed to come from a double Viking burial.

The finder, Daniel Crowe, is not the first in his family to make a discovery like this. In December 2018, his father, John Crowe, and fellow detectorist Craig Evans found the only other pair of Viking oval brooches ever discovered on the island.

The new collection was declared Treasure by the Isle of Man Coroner for Inquests, and Manx National Heritage announced it on November 9. Part of it went on display at the Manx Museum in Douglas two days later.

The finds date to around AD 900. Besides the sword, the haul includes three bronze brooches, decorated lead weights, fragments of bronze balance scales, a bronze ladle and an axehead.

Fellow detectorist Rhett Britton helped with the search. He found the axehead, part of the scales and other iron objects.

The sword is the thirteenth Viking sword found on the island. About two-thirds of it survives. X-rays revealed fine silver inlay and twisted silver wire on parts of its hilt, and only two other Manx Viking swords carry comparable decoration.

It is broken, probably on purpose as part of the burial ritual. Some more damage happened later, while it lay in the ground.

Two of the brooches are oval and decorated with interlocking animals, a distinctive feature of Viking art. Brooches like these were usually worn by women.

The pair found by John Crowe and Craig Evans in 2018 dates to around AD 900 to 950. The new pair could be about 50 years older, which would make it potential evidence of the earliest known female Viking Age burial on the Isle of Man.

Oval brooches were particularly common in the Viking homelands and are seen almost as national dress.

In 2020, Manx National Heritage said their absence from the island until the 2018 find had led to theories that only men from Scandinavia settled there in the early Viking Age.

The third brooch was originally gilded. It has spiral decoration and a glass center, and it is the first of its kind found on the island.

Jewelry typically associated with women, found alongside a sword traditionally associated with men, raises a possibility. The objects may come from a double burial, or from separate graves of the same period.

The site was disturbed at some point over the last thousand years, so the exact circumstances are still uncertain.

At the site of the 2018 brooches, archaeologists from York Archaeological Trust carried out a small excavation but found no grave.

The decorated lead weights and bronze scales would have been used to weigh precious metals and coins during trade. The weights are the first of their type found on the Isle of Man.

Silver and coins also turn up in hoards across the Viking world, like a buried 10th-century hoard that revealed vast Viking trade networks.

One weight carries a bronze fitting, possibly taken from a small chest or a religious object. Its art style is typical of Britain and Ireland at the time, which suggests the settlers reused objects from other cultures.

The ladle, perhaps used at feasts or ceremonies, is another type of object never recorded before on the island.

“This is an extraordinary discovery and one of the most significant groups of Viking Age objects found on the Isle of Man,” said Allison Fox, Curator for Archaeology at Manx National Heritage.

Crowe chose not to clean the objects and handed them over in the state they came out of the ground. That kept traces of evidence that could otherwise have been lost.

His father and Evans did the same in 2018. In 2020, Fox said this mattered because the brooches were fragile and small fragments of textiles from the clothes the woman was buried in might still survive.

This time, before conservation began, the radiology team at Manx Care scanned the objects. The scans looked beneath layers of compacted soil and guided the conservator in uncovering and preserving the objects.

Detectorists elsewhere have made similar finds, such as the hiker with a metal detector who found a Viking treasure hoard and the detectorist who found Finland’s largest Viking Age silver hoard.

Manx National Heritage has not said exactly where the objects were found, only that the landowner cooperated. It also has not given a date for the discovery.

Conservation and research are still underway, and they may reveal more about who owned these objects. Several of them are the first of their kind on the island, so they offer a rare look at early Viking settlement, burial and daily life there.

Visitors can see a selection of the finds in the Viking Gallery of the Manx Museum.

The information was obtained from Manx National Heritage and its 2020 announcement on the earlier brooches.

#6333. The 7 Best Miter Saws for Cutting Precise, Accurate Angles

These crosscutting models, including our top choice from Bosch, make possible an endless array of woodworking projects.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Not too long ago, making precise angled cuts meant using a simple miterbox—a block with precut 90- and 45-degree slots—and a squat little saw with more teeth than a piranha. Those old-school setups still have their place, especially for ultra-clean trim cuts without tearout, but they’ve largely been replaced by the more powerful and versatile miter saw.

When it comes to angled cuts for trim, framing, or furniture, few tools match a good miter saw. A circular blade mounted on a hinged, pivoting arm delivers fast, consistent, and precise cuts at a wide range of angles—something handsaws and circular saws can’t replicate as easily.

The best models combine clean cutting power with accurate miter and bevel adjustments, smooth sliding action, and enough stability to stay precise while cutting dense wood. Features like clear cutline indicators, effective dust collection, and easily adjustable fences also make a huge difference when you’re making cuts all day.

Whether you’re building a garden bed or installing window trim, a miter saw is the fastest way to get accurate, repeatable results.

When selecting potential options for the original version of this article, author Alex Rennie, a former residential and commercial carpenter in New York City, first put together a rough collection of options based on brands and saw types he had found to be most useful to him over the years. After paring that list down, he put each saw through a comprehensive series of tests.

Paul Smith updated this article most recently with the Milwaukee M18 FUEL 18V Sliding Compound Miter Saw, which impressed him during testing. He is in the process of testing more models and will update this article with the results of those tests when they are available. In the meantime, those models are included below as recommended miter saws based on reputation, product specs, features, price point, and online customer reviews.

Unlike most sliding saws that use rails to slide the blade forward and backward, this Bosch miter saw uses an axial-arm mechanism that eliminates the need for rear clearance. This unique design (also used by this Bosch model) allows the saw to take up considerably less space on your workbench without compromising overall cut capacity.

We loved the lever locks that secure the arm in place during transport (although we weren’t as much of a fan of the saw’s hefty 65-pound weight), and the smoothness of the arm, combined with the rubber handle grip, made this an especially comfortable saw to operate.

It’s worth noting that while the clear blade guard (compared to the black of the DeWalt models) provides a clearer view of the cutline, this saw lacks a shadow or laser line feature.

What the Skil 10-inch dual-bevel miter saw lacks in refinement—things like pro-level build quality, multiple bevel detents, and high-end dust collection—it makes up for in capability and cost. At about half the price of most major brands, it delivers consistently clean cuts on a stable, well-constructed turntable.

The motor spins the blade up to 4,800 rpm quickly, so there’s little wait between cuts. In use, cuts were smooth along the rails as I cut through 2x12s, with no tearout or flyaway pieces. The saw is capable of bevels up to 48 degrees left and 45 degrees right—important if you’re making compound miter cuts for things like crown molding. There is a preset detent at 45 degrees left—a common cutting angle—but any bevel angle in between is easily locked down via the rear bevel knob. Even so, it proved accurate across those settings—I had no trouble dialing in compound miters—cuts that employ both miter and bevel cuts—for crown molding that lined up cleanly from both sides.

Ergonomics are a highlight. The trigger sits naturally within the grip, and it’s the only saw I tested that feels equally comfortable left- or right-handed. That might seem minor, but when you’re stretched out on a tricky compound cut, being able to switch hands makes a real difference. Finally, at less than 50 pounds, this saw is no trouble to move around your yard during setup changes or throw in your truck at the end of the day.

This dual-bevel, 10-inch saw packs a lot of power and features into one relatively small and comparatively inexpensive package. With nine positive miter stops and a cutting capacity of 12 inches on the bed, you’ll get up to 500 cuts on a single battery charge.

LED line indicators ensure precision, and a bevel pivot that's as easy to access as it is to operate rounds out this saw's top features. While it's not the most powerful saw, even compared to other cordless options, this one holds its own among the arguably bigger names that populate this list in every other way.

This DeWalt miter saw provides serious power and performance. We found that it maintained speed and power really well during our cut tests, but because it’s cordless, you don’t need to sacrifice mobility when you’re working with it.

The included stabilizer bar ensured that the saw felt sturdy and stable while we cut, and the included LED work light created a convenient, precise shadow line to maximize accuracy. We also appreciated how well the instruction manual walked us through all the different operations, giving us comprehensive instructions on a variety of cuts.

At a little over 50 pounds (without the 20-volt battery, which you’ll have to buy separately) and with a top-mounted carrying handle, this was one of the easier saws to transport during testing. Plus, this saw’s dust port was located on the side, instead of the rear, which made it easier to fit on a smaller workbench.

With dual-bevel capabilities, smooth gliding rails, and user-friendly controls and adjustment knobs, this cordless powerhouse handles everything from 13.5-inch-wide cuts to 6.5-inch-tall baseboards.

This saw won’t be your go-to if you’re working with large lumber. Nothing bigger than a 2x4 is recommended here, but if that type of work isn’t on your horizon, this saw is as easy to maneuver as it is to operate.

Its small size and extremely accurate blade make it ideal for using indoors to cut trim, flooring, and picture framing. And at just over 14 pounds, it’s a breeze to move from room to room as you work. We also like the gooseneck type of LED built into the blade housing for throwing light on your entire cut. And the 64-tooth blade delivers a clean, precise cut every time.

If you believe you get what you pay for, this Makita 8-1/2-inch miter saw makes the case. Tools should solve problems—and this one addresses a big one in its category: size versus capability. A 12-inch saw powers through 4x4s but is heavy and space-hungry; a compact 6-inch is portable but limited. This Makita saw lands squarely in between.

This 40-volt cordless saw delivers corded-level power in a lighter package—roughly 10 to 20 pounds less than larger models—while still handling 12-inch crosscuts. Its forward-facing rails save valuable workspace, letting it sit flush against a wall without the usual rear clearance.

Build quality stands out immediately. The heavy aluminum turntable feels rigid under load, with precise detents that lock in smoothly at common angles—no fighting to find your mark. Preset bevel stops on both sides add convenience, and the front-mounted bevel lock means no awkward reaching over the saw.

Makita also includes dual dust collection options: a standard bag or a ducted port for a dedicated system. Pair it with Makita’s AWS technology and pulling the trigger wirelessly activates a compatible vacuum—an easy, thoughtful upgrade for shop workflow.

Prior to using this saw, I read that some users had issues with the out-of-the-box accuracy of the table in relation to the blade. This situation is problematic when cutting trim, for instance, because it needs to fit perfectly.

I personally experienced none of that. I cut a variety of woods with this saw—from 2x10s to MDF trim—and the results completely satisfied me. Cuts were clean, splinter-free, and above all, accurate at connection.

The saw is powerful, thanks in part to its brushless motor and impressive battery, which Milwaukee claims makes 330 cuts per charge, but I honestly ran out of wood before that number (and according to the battery indicators, I still had half a charge remaining).

Milwaukee puts a lot of effort into getting its shadow line system clear and precise, and I appreciate that when it comes to eyeing up my cuts. As an added bonus, I find the LED field is the best of any saw I’ve used, cordless or otherwise. My only complaints are that the rear bevel is a little clunky to maneuver and the table extenders have an underwhelming feel to them. If you’re expanding your Milwaukee cordless platform, this saw is a great add.

A few of our readers gave us grief earlier this year for overlooking Evolution’s jobsite table saw on our list of the best table saws, so I called one in. I ran a piece of old angle iron through it before proceeding to cut hardwood, plywood, and pine trim with minimal tearout. My takeaway was that the saw lived up to the hype. Now, I’m curious how Evolution’s 10-inch miter saw handles the same materials.

I’ll start with framing lumber and trim to see how accurately the saw repeats miters and how cleanly it cuts in both bevel directions. Then, I’ll cut some aluminum angle stock and light-gauge steel tubing before moving on to hardwood with the same blade. I want to see how much cleanup each piece of metal needs and whether that last pair of hardwood miters fits together as neatly as the first pair of standard lumber and pine base molding. All throughout, I’ll be looking at standard saw features, as well, including motor power, build quality, table detents, LED lighting or shadow lines, and dust collection.

The three main types of miter saws are compound, dual compound, and sliding. Each variation performs specific functions and cuts better than the others, so it’s important that you understand their differences and also have a decent idea of how you plan on using your saw.

In addition to lowering straight down for perpendicular crosscuts, the blade of a compound miter saw also pivots from side to side for angled “miter” cuts, and it tilts to one side for bevel cuts. A “compound” cut utilizes both of these functions in one motion and is commonly used to create things like picture frames or to cut crown molding for installation.

Instead of tilting to only one side for bevel cuts, dual compound saws (also called “double” or “double-bevel” compound saws) tilt in both directions. This makes work much faster than using a standard compound saw because while a compound saw technically makes all the same cuts as a dual compound saw, its single-bevel design means you spend more time flipping workpieces around to cut opposite angles.

These two non-sliding types are solid options for homeowners who want a reasonably compact and portable machine.

A standard compound miter saw drops straight down onto the board. It’s great for narrow stock but limited by the diameter of the blade. A sliding compound miter saw adds rails that let the blade travel forward and backward during the course of the cut. This feature dramatically increases the width of material the saw can handle—making it possible to cut wider boards in a single pass. If you’re cutting a lot of shelving, flooring, or wide trim, a sliding miter saw, such as the DeWalt 20V MAX XR Dual-Bevel Sliding Miter Saw, is usually worth the extra cost and size.

When shopping for a miter saw, you’ll also need to decide what type of power source you prefer.

Cordless miter saws have improved dramatically over the last few years, mostly due to the evolution of high-capacity lithium-ion batteries and the inclusion of brushless motors. Today’s 18- and 20-volt models offer plenty of power for trim work and general carpentry without sacrificing the portability that makes cordless power tools appealing in the first place.

I like knowing I can set up the saw anywhere and get to work without worrying about finding power or running an extension cord through an open door or window. That said, corded saws still hold the edge when it comes to cutting ability and run time.

Most miter saws come with 10- or 12-inch blades, and that difference has a big impact on what type of cuts and tasks the saw excels at.

A 10-inch saw, such as the Metabo HPT Single Bevel Compound Miter Saw, is typically lighter and easier to move around your shop or from room to room. It’s more than capable of cutting trim, flooring, and smaller dimensional lumber.

A 12-inch saw, on the other hand, gives you significantly more cutting capacity—especially when you’re working with wider boards or tall trim pieces like crown molding. 12-inch saws, like our Best Overall choice, the Bosch GCM12SD Dual-Bevel Sliding Miter Saw, are a bit more awkward to move around the workplace.

A large saw also adds bulk and takes up more room in the shop or truck. But the trade-off to those negatives is that you’re far less likely to run into a job that you simply can’t handle. I’d rather deal with the extra footprint than discover upon starting a project that my saw is undersized. If you have the space, it’s often better to size up.

Blade speed, measured in rpm (revolutions per minute), is another important performance indicator. Most miter saws operate between 3,000 and 5,500 rpm, and naturally, higher speeds increase your cutting efficiency. Some saws, like the Hilti Nuron 22V miter saw, even allow you to customize your speed to a specific task, which makes it uniquely versatile.

That said, the relationship between the saw blade diameter and rpm makes comparing the speed of two miter saws a little more complex. Two saws running at the same rpm, but using different-sized blades—let’s say 7¼-inch and 12-inch—will not cut at the same speed. That’s because even though the center of each blade is spinning at the same speed, the outer edge of the 12-inch blade will turn faster than the edge of the 7¼-inch one.

Things get even more complicated when we bring the blade’s tooth count into the mix, with higher-tooth blades reducing speed. As a beginner, you can drive yourself a little crazy trying to determine the perfect combination of blade factors, so I’d recommend relying on your saw’s instruction manual for basic guidance.

Modern miter saws often include features designed to help you cut more accurately and consistently. Some use laser guides to project the cut line, while others use LED systems that cast a shadow from the blade, so you can see exactly where it will land. Detents at common angle stops around the saw table—like 22.5 degrees and 45 degrees—also make it faster to dial in repeated cuts. These features aren’t essential, but they make a noticeable difference when you’re making dozens of cuts in a row.

Paul Russell Smith is a former NYC ironworker turned screenwriter (Grace Point) and home renovation specialist. When he’s not working, he enjoys hiking, pedestrian beer, and cooking over a live fire. His self-proclaimed spirit animal is the English Bulldog.
