#6252. Trump administration ups ante on aviation funds after ground stop

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they said old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.

The increased allotment, which the administration officials didn’t fully flesh out, comes after the nation’s air traffic control system experienced “instability” in its radar and communications at certain facilities earlier in the day, Duffy told reporters.

He said “inconsistency in the data” being issued by those systems led to implementation of the nationwide ground stop, saying the order was given out of “an abundance of caution” before being lifted about four hours later.

During a Friday night White House briefing, Duffy and Mullin explained the issues were driven by “an incredibly old air traffic control system.”

Earlier in the day, the stoppage had caused mass confusion and raised questions about potential terror attacks, or artificial intelligence breakouts resulting from new software the agency is rolling out. While Mullin said “we’re not ruling out anything,” he explained that “the public was never at danger through this process.”

Still, Duffy called the incident “an emergency” while calling for additional modernization funds.

“This is an emergency,” he said. “I want $50 billion. President Trump is a builder. He’s going to build this network and deliver for the American people. But the president can’t deliver for America unless the Congress delivers the money to make it happen.”

The latest figure is $19.1 billion higher than the figure Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought called on congressional appropriators to approve in a Thursday letter.

Mullin said the new $50 billion figure was an administration estimate for a “complete overhaul of the system” which has been going through a “patchwork” upgrade process that may have overwhelmed the older equipment still being used.

“We need someone to come in and build the whole system," Mullin said. "Nickel and diming it together does not work."

Thursday’s call for $30.1 billion echoes a White House-backed bill that Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced in September, which would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $2 billion for "cloud computing and national airspace system telecommunications."

Those funds would come after $12.5 billion allocated to the effort through the July 2025 reconciliation law that Duffy and Vought called a “down-payment."

Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee Republicans touted those already-appropriated funds in a social media post. They pointed to $1.9 billion provided in the reconciliation law that would go toward upgrading air route traffic control centers, which guide planes across long distances after departure and which the FAA had cited as the cause of the problem.

The 22 air route traffic control centers across the country guide aircraft using instrument-dependent flight plans. Under such plans, pilots use instruments, electronic navigation and air traffic control assistance to guide them and maintain separation from other aircraft in certain airspaces.

The committee’s majority said Friday's outage highlighted the need to prioritize modernization of the air route traffic control centers, arguing that President Lyndon B. Johnson was in office the last time a new one was built.

Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., said in a statement Friday night that the panel is looking into FAA and airspace telecommunications issues.

“Technology issues related to how planes communicate through primary frequencies, backup frequencies, and other issues will be something the Commerce Committee will be reviewing,” Cantwell said.

Cantwell is poised to take the committee's gavel come January as Democrats assume the majority in the Senate.

In a joint statement Friday night, House Transportation and Infrastructure Chairman Sam Graves, R-Mo., and ranking member Rick Larsen, D-Wash., called the communication failures “concerning” and said their committee would “thoroughly review the issues that led to this nationwide ground stop.”

Both committees have also been in monthslong negotiations over dueling aviation safety bills responding to the January 2025 midair collision near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport that killed 67 people.

At issue in those negotiations is which location transmission technology should be mandated to aid in air traffic control operations and allow aircraft to maintain appropriate distance. Leaders have said they hope to reach a deal in the lame-duck session.

#6251. Do You Trust Your Own Intuition? Here’s How You Sharpen It—And Win at Life, Researchers Say

It’s all about honing your instincts through practice and experience.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

Think about the phrase “it’s just like riding a bicycle.” At first, it’s hard, and you have to pay attention to what you’re doing, but after you’ve practiced for many hours, bike riding becomes so natural you don’t even have to think about it; you just hop on and go. In fact, you can hardly explain how you learned in the first place or exactly how you’re keeping your balance as you pedal on. You just trust your body to do it. The same applies to cognitive activities: As a child, you had to really think about how to arrive at the answer of 2+2, but now, you just know it’s four, without thinking.

Intuition is about finding the solution automatically and without deep thought, says Wim De Neys, a cognitive psychologist and CNRS research professor at the University of Paris. At its core, your intuition is a behavior your brain develops based on patterns and experiences over time, a kind of automation for something you’ve done countless times. That’s why intuition is often linked to expertise. Trusting your gut may sound ill-advised, so why wouldn’t you want to think things through? But it turns out that generating your instincts for decision-making can both help you make the right choice in times of confusion and stress, and also free up mental resources for other tasks.

So, can you train your intuition to sense better choices?

Well, it’s not that simple, according to De Neys, whose research focuses on how intuitive and deliberate thinking develops over our lifetimes. You can’t sidestep the deep reflection needed to build the foundation of your intuitions. But you can tap into them in a more meaningful way, especially over time.

“Having gut feelings and intuition and even valid intuitions, there’s science to back it up,” De Neys says. “It exists, but it’s always tied to expertise, and expertise means it’s something that you’ve done a lot.”

Intuition isn’t some overall sense; instead it’s tied to one area of expertise, like an interviewer being able to pick up on the candidate who’ll be the right fit for the job, or an experienced doctor delivering a diagnosis. While you won’t have expert intuition about everything under the sun, there are a few ways you can boost your own decision-making.

First, you need to get better at pattern matching, and that means practice. Intuition is tied to pattern-matching, Jeff Larsen, PhD, a professor of psychology at the University of Tennessee, explains. For example, chess masters earn their distinction by practicing so much that when they see the board, they don’t have to stop and think about what the two or three best moves will be. Others with less expertise may watch a game and think, “that was a silly move,” but they don’t realize the master player has spent years building up pattern recognition, or an accurate gut feeling, Larsen explains.

Second, stop second-guessing your intuition. You can do this by asking yourself, “How might I be wrong?” One approach is to ask a friend who may disagree with you or might have an outside perspective. This can also help you understand that, often, an instinctual choice you made in the heat of the moment is correct. Even if the choice isn’t exactly right, it’s probably good enough to keep you safe. For example, when you’re driving down the interstate, you have some intuition about whether you can make a lane change or not, and whether you need to slow down or speed up to avoid an accident. Thinking about the consequences of your decision-making can also help give you more confidence in your intuition.

Sometimes you have to trust your gut on a truly life-changing decision. When it comes to marriage, the information overload can sometimes feel overwhelming. However, when it comes to close relationships, you’ve presumably experienced many behavioral exchanges with your partner, and this allows for substantial information-gathering to “feed your gut,” Michael Olson, PhD, a professor of psychology at the University of Tennessee, explains.

Since you can’t possibly keep this massive load of information in your conscious memory at all times, it translates into a neat summary of all those behavioral exchanges. Now you have a gut feeling that this person is right for you—or not.

And the research agrees. A study Olson coauthored, published in Science, found that the “explicit,” or “conscious” evaluations couples in the study made of their partners while in the so-called initial “honeymoon stage” didn’t mean as much when stretched over four years. Instead, those who reported positive gut feelings over this time period had a more accurate idea of their happiness in their relationship.

Your gut doesn’t just extend to your love life. Trusting it can also help you to be successful in business. Elizabeth Rea, an evidentiary clairvoyant psychic medium, now teaches established founders and CEOs to tap into their own intuitions, through her company, Insightful. As a medium, Rea has also assisted U.S. federal special agents investigating cold murder cases.

When working with clients, she asks them to relax what they consciously believe. Sometimes so-called gut feelings may come to us in the form of chills down our spine or another physical sensation. But since we’re living in a left-brained culture that prizes making decisions using logic and analysis, those instincts often get passed off as coincidences and ignored, Rea says. Sometimes, gut feelings may also be ignored because of self-doubt. Your intuition often whispers to you, she tells clients. Honing these signals will help you improve your self-trust—thereby improving your intuition.

Overall, training yourself to trust your intuition will help you become a better decision-maker. You’ll make the right choices without the agonizing process of picking through pros and cons and running scenarios in your brain for days on end.

“It’s a lot more cost-efficient if we can offload [decision-making] to our intuition,” De Neys says. “Often that’s going to be helpful because then it frees up resources for something else that might be more important at that point in time.”

#6250. This 9-Year-Old Owns Dozens of Vintage Toilets. He May Have Found His Calling in Plumbing—and Is Inspiring Others.

The U.S. is facing a trades crisis. Fostering some unique hobbies may be the fix we desperately need.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

Like most kids his age, 9-year-old Damian Skaer loves YouTube. Unlike most kids his age, Damian also loves toilets, a passion he discovered on the social media platform.

Now, he’s a social media star himself, showing off his growing collection of vintage toilets to hundreds of thousands of followers across TikTok and Instagram: a pale yellow 1965 American Standard Cadet, a robin’s egg-blue 1963 Crane Oxford, and a 1972 Kohler Wellworth the color of an army tank. Standing on the 11-toilet, fully plumbed platform his dad built in the family’s Eastern Washington backyard, Damian points out their trapways, the fill valves, the siphon jets, the lid bolts, and, of course, the pièce de resistance—the flush.

Roger Skaer, Damian’s dad, says his son’s obsession began a few years ago. “He stumbled across these plumbers on YouTube who replace toilets, test them, fix them, and, man, he just loves watching videos of people working on toilets,” Roger says. “There’s been a lot of engineering behind toilet evolution over the last 100 years, and he’s fascinated by it.”

Damian’s collection began when he found a couple of old toilets in his grandparents’ barn. Since then, he has amassed about 40, according to Roger. Each week, new models arrive from brands looking to collaborate with the 9-year-old.

While the topic of young people and screens continues to cause serious consternation among adults, for some kids, they’re serving as an introduction to the skilled trades, occupations like carpentry, welding, and plumbing that have struggled to attract and retain new talent. According to a 2026 National Association of House Builders survey, only 6 percent of young adults 18 to 25 planned to pursue a career in construction trades.

But a crop of young social media influencers are bucking that trend. Guiseppe D’Anna has been working on cars at his dad’s collision repair shop since he was six; today Guiseppe’s Garage has a quarter-million followers on YouTube, and the automotive wunderkind is on “a mission to help shape the next generation of gearheads.” British woodworker Gabriel River Clark has been creating DIY content since he was 12, crafting anything from dinnerware to toys to home decor. On TikTok, 10-year-old Jackson Laux, a.k.a. Just a Jackson Thing, delights his roughly million followers with his deep knowledge of vintage tractors and mowers.

This kind of early exposure is vital to promoting trade occupations, says Paul Goodrum, PhD, a professor in Construction Engineering and Management at the University of Colorado Boulder. While lots of kids used to learn these skills in high school shop or career tech classes, over the past few decades, policy makers and administrators have phased vocational educational courses out of high school curriculums, emphasizing core academic subjects and college readiness instead. The best vocational programs, according to Goodrum, tend to exist in alternative schools for students with behavioral challenges.

“There is a bit of a disconnect between how we measure the quality of our schools and what the economy and the workforce needs in this country,” he says. “As an industry, we really need to be trying to more actively expose kids to these career paths not just in high school but middle school too.”

But it’s a vicious cycle, Goodrum says: fewer trades workers mean fewer teachers to teach vocational classes, “and how do you convince someone to give up a really high-paying job to go teach high school?”

The shortage of skilled workers is creating headaches for more than just hiring managers. A reduced workforce is causing construction project costs to soar and go over schedule. It’s also turning worksites into danger zones, as understaffed crews are working longer hours at a brutal pace. In 2024, construction workers accounted for about one in five workplace deaths in the country.

Most workers who end up in trade occupations do so later in life, often as a second career. The average age of an apprentice in a construction program is 28, for instance, while plumbing and electrical apprentices are often pushing 40.

“For so long we nurtured this culture saying you’ve got to go to college and get this degree or that degree, and if you end up working in construction it was because you somehow failed,” says Roger Skaer, a trained carpenter. “I think it’s a product of a long-lived, misguided representation of what success should look like.”

Recently, young people have started to question that college-or-bust narrative. Between 2020 and 2025, enrollment in two-year vocational or trade schools grew by almost 20 percent. And while the trades have their own difficulties—dangerous work conditions, wear and tear on the body—they offer something lots of other fields can’t right now: job security. According to the New Hampshire–based nonprofit Bring Back the Trades, more than 1.4 million trade jobs will be vacant in 2030.

Roger is confident that eventually Damian will fill one of those positions. “Right now, he’s saying plumber, I’m thinking maybe a toilet designer,” he says, explaining that Damian’s been angling for a 3D printer so that he can build his own commodes. “I truly feel he's going to be in some kind of trade or hands-on craftwork.”

And if toilets don’t pan out, Damian has a backup hobby: washer and dryer installation and repair.

Scientists are perplexed at discovering the world's deepest explosive volcanic eruption at Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A submersible mission to the deepest ocean trench on Earth has made a shocking discovery: the deepest pyroclastic volcanic flow ever found on the planet, in a place geologists didn't expect to see any volcanic activity.

This evidence of a violent undersea eruption was found 20,000 feet (6,000 meters) below the ocean surface on the walls of the Challenger Deep, the deepest point of the Mariana Trench and the deepest part of the ocean. It was a "complete surprise," said Robert Stern, a professor emeritus of geosciences at the University of Texas at Dallas and first author of a new study describing the discovery.

Typically, volcanic activity doesn't occur that close to an ocean trench, Stern told Live Science. And given the site's extreme depth, the lava that made the flow must have had some very strange chemistry. Normally, the intense pressure of seawater at these depths would prevent an explosive eruption, instead favoring a goopier, seeping type of flow. But the flows seen on the edge of the Challenger Deep were similar to the explosive, roiling gases that coated Pompeii in ash in A.D. 79.

"It's not something that as a geoscientist I would have said would be predicted," said Sune Nielsen, a geochemist at the University of Lorraine in France who was not involved in the study. "Very far from it."

A fish in the genus Pseudoliparis in an image taken during during a dive by the Jason/Medea ROV at 20,659 feet (6,297 m).

The Challenger Deep is in the remote western Pacific at the southern end of the Mariana Trench. There, the Pacific oceanic plate pushes under the Mariana oceanic plate in a process called subduction. At the trench where the two plates meet, the ocean floor plunges down 6.8 miles (10.9 kilometers). Mount Everest could fit in the chasm, with room to spare.

Geoscientists aren't sure why the trench is so dizzyingly deep, but they have turned up some clues. For instance, there is a tear in the Pacific Plate that allows one narrow strip of the plate to subduct particularly rapidly. The curvature of the plate is also very steep, perhaps because the rocks of the Mariana and Pacific plates aren't very strongly connected to each other, allowing the Pacific Plate to dive steeply and flex freely.

The new findings, reported Monday (Nov. 23) in the journal Frontiers in Earth Science, suggest that volcanism and magma also may play a role, Stern said. The researchers were exploring a segment of the Challenger Deep's forearc, a roughly 120-mile-wide (200 km) expanse that sits between the trench itself and the volcanic arc created by the subduction zone. These volcanic arcs are standard subduction zone features; for example, Mount St. Helens and Mount Rainier are part of the volcanic arc of the Cascadia subduction zone in the Pacific Northwest.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

But though there are some volcanoes north of Challenger Deep along the Mariana Trench, the Challenger Deep segment of the trench is odd in that there is not an organized volcanic arc there. Instead, there's an ocean ridge. Regardless, the space between this ridge and the trench was expected to be volcanically quiet because there is not usually enough heat in that region of a subduction zone to melt magma.

Nevertheless, the cameras on the deep-diving remotely operated vehicle Jason/Medea, which went to the site in 2014, caught strange, pancake-like rock features at three different spots in a 60-mile (100 km) stretch of the trench. Samples brought on board the ship revealed rock embedded with volcanic glass and a pyroclastic flow texture.

A sea cucumber in an image from the Jason/Medea dive at 12,726 feet (3879 m).

The researchers are currently getting the rock dated, but volcanic glass usually erodes quickly in the ocean, Stern said, so the presence of glass suggests the eruptions were fairly recent. "They're not yesterday," he said, "but I don't think they're a million years old."

The pressure of the water at the depths of the flows is equivalent to 592 atmospheres of Earth stacked on top of one another. Typically, that kind of pressure keeps a lid on the dissolved water and carbon dioxide in magma that expands rapidly to cause explosive eruptions. Thus, Stern said, the eruptions by the Challenger Deep may have been driven by a supercritical fluid ‪—‬ a weird state sort of in between a gas and a liquid.

"We just don’t know how those magmas will behave at those water depths," said Stephen Self, a volcanologist at the University of California, Berkeley, who was not involved in the study.

The mission's observations also suggest that the crust of this region is extending, or stretching, in two different ways. To the east, the stretch is caused by a mechanical pulling apart of the crust. To the west, volcanic eruptions are stretching the crust. It's a perplexing finding, Nielsen said, without a clear explanation.

Stern and his colleagues suspect that the two plates are starting a new subduction zone in this western part. That would be an exciting finding; subduction zones move around over tens of millions of years, and researchers don't know much about how new ones start. The geochemical studies of the rocks that Stern and his team pulled up could answer questions about where the lava that made the pyroclastic flows came from and why this bizarre region can generate magma where none should be.

"This region is really, really unusual for our planet, and there is quite a bit of, 'What, really? Wait, how is that? OK, yeah, I guess maybe.'" Nielsen said. "So obviously, I find it super interesting."

Stern, R. J., Pujana, I., Anderson, M. K., Chin, E., Dygert, N., Harigane, Y., Le Roux, V., Leybourne, M., Ohara, Y., Okumura, T., Segee-Wright, G., & Etheridge, E. (n.d.). ROVing in the deep: Tectonic and magmatic complexities of the challenger deep forearc segment, southern mariana convergent margin. Frontiers in Earth Science, 14, 1929806. https://doi.org/10.3389/feart.2026.1929806

Stephanie Pappas is a contributing writer for Live Science, covering topics ranging from geoscience to archaeology to the human brain and behavior. She was previously a senior writer for Live Science but is now a freelancer based in Denver, Colorado, and regularly contributes to Scientific American and The Monitor, the monthly magazine of the American Psychological Association. Stephanie received a bachelor's degree in psychology from the University of South Carolina and a graduate certificate in science communication from the University of California, Santa Cruz.

Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.

Explanation: What creates the colors in Jupiter's clouds? No one is sure. The thick atmosphere of Jupiter is mostly hydrogen and helium, elements which are colorless at the low temperatures of the Jovian cloud tops. Which trace molecules provide the colors remains a topic of research, although small amounts of ammonium hydrosulfide are one leading candidate. What is clear from the featured color-enhanced image -- and many similar images -- is that lighter clouds are typically higher up than darker ones. Pictured, light clouds swirl around reddish regions toward the lower right, while they appear to cover over some darker domains on the upper right. The featured image was taken by the robotic Juno spacecraft in 2018 during its 14th low pass over Jupiter. Juno continues in its looping elliptical orbit, swooping near the huge planet every 33 days and exploring a slightly different sector each time around.Tomorrow's picture: emerging darkness

#6247. How I Got My Visa to France

I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010. Friends I had met back in Thailand showed me around the area and introduced me to French culture. It was my first time in France and I loved the food, the wine, and the people.

But that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées. The lights, the energy, the mystique! There was magic in the air. I felt like I had known the city my entire life and I was simply returning home.

Since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart. Over the years, I spent countless visits exploring France and Paris in particular. I’ve run tours in the city and I spent a few months living there in 2019.

Last August, after yet another sojourn, I thought to myself, “What if I moved back?”

I was growing a bit tired of the NYC dating scene, the rising cost of living, and felt like, creatively, I was in a rut. With AI coming for creators like me and the industry changing, I was a little lost on what, career-wise, would come next.

And Paris seemed like the best place to go.

It’s cheaper than NYC, I had friends there already, I’ve always wanted to learn French, it would make a great base for exploring Europe, and I could start writing my next book there. There’s nothing like a change in scenery to get the creativity flowing!

But the question remained: how do you move to France?

After all, they don’t have a digital nomad visa, and you’re limited to three months if you visit on your regular Schengen tourist visa.

Well, it turns out that it’s not actually that hard. (And while I can only speak for Americans, I suspect the criteria are similar for Canadians, Aussies, Kiwis, and other “developed” nations.)

If you want to move to France, you have four main options:

The student visa is pretty straightforward. You need to enroll in a full-time university program and show you have enough funds to support yourself (around 600 Euros per month). A friend is currently there on this visa, as she is doing a nine-month intensive French program to become fluent. You still have to apply for the visa, but if you’re enrolled in an accredited school, you’ll likely get approved. Another benefit to this visa is that you can work part-time on it!

But this visa is contingent on being in school, so if you leave or quit, it’s voided. However, when you are done, you can change this to a “job seeker” visa, which can give you up to another six months in France (or more depending on how long your program was).

I thought about applying for the entrepreneur visa, but the application process is pretty complex and can take months to be approved. You have to set up your business in France — and that is a lot of paperwork. You have to show that your business makes money, has clients (at least one of them being French), and can support you full-time (you have to make at least the French minimum wage). They will scrutinize your assets and financials a lot and you’ll need to register your business in France and pay French taxes.

Additionally, France offers a talent visa. If you’re an expert in your field (with verifiable accreditations and accolades), this could be a good visa to apply for, especially if you plan to stay in France for a long time and want to physically work there. But, again, you’ll need to have some source of income and plan to do physical business in France. If you’re not an academic but someone in the arts, you have to show how you are going to add to the “culture of France” in some way.

While I would meet the requirements for both those visas, the process for either would have been time-consuming, and, since I’m not sure France is going to be my forever home, I decided not to go through that process.

So I went with the long-term visitor visa, officially called VLS-TS visiteur. This allows me to stay up to 12 months in France and is renewable in the country. It does come with a lot of restrictions, however: I can’t physically work here and I am not allowed into the French social welfare system.

It’s also the visa a lot of Americans (and most retirees) are coming in on. If you have passive income or retirement savings and just want to live in France, this is a good option for you. It allows you to set up a bank account and it can be renewed pretty much indefinitely.

The paperwork for this visa (which I’ll get into in a bit) essentially comes down to whether or not you can support yourself. French authorities want to make sure you won’t be a burden on the system.

My biggest question centered around whether or not I could “work” on this visa. A lot of creators and digital nomads are applying for — and getting — this visa.

But remember: you aren’t allowed to work on this visa so how are you going to work if you can’t work?

So let me take a moment to talk about “work” from a legal standpoint.

As I mentioned, there’s no digital nomad visa that allows you to work in France. And the French tax office said last July that remote work is considered taxable — but there are no official laws that say so. That’s just their opinion and there’s been no progress in codifying that opinion. In fact, my visa doesn’t even come with a tax number, so I can’t be taxed. I couldn’t pay taxes even if I wanted to.

The visa office asks how you’ll support yourself when you are in France and one of the sources of income they accept is “income from work.” I was very open that my means of support would be the income from this blog and my books.

The system there really hasn’t caught up to remote work. It still defines “work” as something you do physically that could take away a job from a French person.

So could I run walking tours in Paris? Nope. Could you work at a café? Nope.

But does writing this blog post count as work? After all, no one is paying for it. It’s a free resource. Does going to a café to work on the next great American novel count? What about my weekly newsletter that has affiliate links (that generate income) in it? Is writing that considered work?

The gray area is considerable, so the best thing to do is to talk to a lawyer. I recommend Daniel Tostado (yes, that’s his real name), one of the biggest American-French immigration lawyers in Paris. He has a huge law firm and regularly meets with government officials to clarify the rules on this. He gave me some solid advice.

For this long-term visitor visa, the application process is pretty easy. You go to the French government website, fill out your application, take the application number to the TLScontact website, and make an appointment. (France outsources the appointment process to this company, which then sends everything to the French consulate for approval.)

The main things you’ll want to demonstrate are that you have accommodation for 90 days on your application and enough income to support yourself. They just want to make sure you aren’t going to be a burden on the system. I went overboard. Here’s what I brought to my appointment:

I didn’t need the second bank account, tax returns, or W-2 (they weren’t required) but the woman at the appointment said the more proof you had the better and it wouldn’t hurt. And another friend who got this visa didn’t bring anything beyond what was asked in the application form. But I wanted to take no chances!

At the appointment, the staff double-checks your paperwork, takes your biometric data, collects the fees, and then sends your passport to the embassy for processing. Officially, it takes up to 15 days to process your visa, but everyone I know seems to get it back within a week.

The worst part was not knowing if you are approved until your passport is returned. While you can track the progress of your application, you don’t know the verdict until your passport is back in your hands. While I was waiting (and anxiously spiraling), I looked on Reddit and found that most denials were for lack of income or issues with their accommodation, which seem to be the two most important things to have perfect on your application.

Once you get your visa back, you can enter France any time after the start date. After you enter, you have 90 days to register your visa with the state (they give you a little QR code with instructions). This allows you to “officially” be on this long-term visa. (It’s a more paperwork kind of thing.)

Once that is done, there’s nothing else to do and you can stay in France (and Europe) until your visa expires!

So, if you’re considering moving to France, these are your options. But, as always, I’m not a lawyer and this is not legal advice. In regard to work and other issues or questions, it’s important that you seek legal counsel and get their expert opinion!

#6245. Americans Are Rethinking What Comes After Death. For Some, the Answer Is Becoming Soil.

The process of grinding up your bones in a “cremulator” may sound grisly, but it’s quickly gaining traction in the death market.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

In the United States, the way we think about death has rapidly changed. For instance, a 2026 National Funeral Directors Association (NFDA) report predicts that cremation will account for more than 64 percent of funerary arrangements this year. Likewise, an NFDA release from 2025 claims that more than 61 percent of consumers are interested in exploring “green funeral” options.

Some of those people are opting for human composting, or natural organic reduction. It doesn’t require high heat generation, it doesn’t take up space like a traditional burial, and it creates a natural source of plant nutrition. It’s a way to truly return to the earth.

In a human composting center, workers place a body into a contained ecosystem along with natural bedding like mulch and hay, and periodically tend to each habitat (similar to how you rotate your compost.) The process that Katrina Spade helped to design at her company—Recompose, based in Seattle—is modeled on one used to compost dead livestock; in testing, she hired a soil scientist to ensure that the heat of the composting process was enough to kill any pathogens. This happens in plant and animal composting, too.

At a similar company, Return Home, the process digests the soft tissues of the body into nutrients in the soil. Then the bones and any medical devices can be removed, and the latter are recycled. The company uses a cremulator, a traditional cremation tool, to grind bones into pieces. Like a coffee grinder or blender, the cremulator’s rotating blades turn larger pieces into smaller ones. The resulting finer particulate of bone is ideal for composting.

Today, people interested in burial have a lot of choices. That’s partly because strict laws and taboos around burying people outside of cemeteries or other designated places are changing. A majority of states allow burial on private property, some with caveats. Embalming is not required across the board. Even the required depth of burial varies a lot, and some states don’t have a depth requirement.

For some people, allowing unembalmed burial on private land isn’t enough. Many people will never own land in a rural enough place to comfortably bury a loved one. Cemeteries have been running out of space for a while, and experts say fewer people want the traditional American ceremonies linked with death, like viewings and services at funeral homes and churches. But that doesn’t mean people don’t want their death to bring closure, a sense of ritual, or a meaningful return to the earth.

Cities have long had unique challenges with human burial because of their population density. Neighborhoods might eventually surround cemeteries on the edge of town by the time they need to expand. Our parklike modern cemeteries date back to just Victorian times, when they were boosted as part of an overall public park movement in the United Kingdom. Even Brooklyn’s iconic Green-Wood Cemetery started as a public park. But while taxes fund parks, cemeteries are often privately owned. When they stop having open spaces to sell, they start losing income. It grows ethically murky very fast.

This is where human composting enters the scene. As a graduate student, Spade first introduced the idea in her architecture thesis in 2013, The Verge reports. She wondered if people in cities might plan to send their dead bodies to clean, organized spaces where caretakers could use nature’s own processes to speed up decomposition—or “recomposition,” as she calls it. This results in an amount of enriched soil, because the human body is full of nutrients like nitrogen, potassium, and phosphate that plants need.

It works a lot like any other composting system, or wild life cycle, such as a decomposing log or whale fall—when dead whales sink and become an instant food source for other creatures. Natural topsoil called humus hosts organisms whose place in the ecosystem is to digest animal and plant matter into soil. On the spectrum of humus decomposers, earthworms fall on the larger end, while microbes and tiny insects fall on the smaller end. Together, they form a food web, with each organism playing a part, like digesting a particular nutrient or a particular size of particle.

“Death market” figures show the overall rise in cremation rates during the COVID-19 pandemic. Cremation results in a small, tangible object that can be buried anytime, without the countdown to decay that even embalming can’t stop. For decades, the practice has been growing in popularity as a more environmental and space-saving way to prepare bodies after death.

But that’s not the end of the story. Traditional cremation requires temperatures of 1,400–1,600 Fahrenheit, the Cremation Association of North America explains. The type of ashes we imagine—where what is left is fine powder with some small shards of bone—is just not possible with a wood fire. While it is possible with coal or maybe an accelerant, at that point, the environmental catch-22 is pretty evident. Traditional cremation is better at saving space than it is at saving the planet—and saving space has had enormous value around the world for thousands of years.

The Financial Times estimates that each traditional cremation in the U.K. in 2018 cost about 150 kilograms of carbon dioxide; that’s more than a one-way flight from Boston to Paris. Traditional funerals cost many thousands of dollars on average, and burying embalmed human bodies in airtight containers has never been an environmentally friendly project to begin with. If you’re thinking about your future, there are more options than ever.

At Return Home, the “immediate need” package costs $5,950. The company also offers another option at the same price: pre-planning your funeral and financing it with a payment plan. At Recompose, the composting service is $7,000, with options for various remembrance services ranging from $500 up to $1,700. These are somewhat in line with current funeral costs, estimated at an average of $8,596, according to US Funerals Online, an industry resource company based in Delaware.

There’s also one wrinkle if you want your body to be composted after your death: Bodies cannot be embalmed before the process starts. The chemicals used in the funeral industry are “not compatible with” the natural decomposition process, Recompose explains, and many are carcinogenic or otherwise toxic. In other words, they aren’t safe to mix into soil that people will take home and use in their yards. If you die while traveling, you will typically be embalmed before you’re transported home.

There’s an interesting split over human composting, particularly evident in Christianity. The Verge’s 2022 article about Return Home leads with an anecdote about Sharon, a woman who had died from complications of multiple sclerosis. She was also a Mormon. True-blue Christians hew to an idea called stewardship, which is the way humankind must care for the earth and environment as cornerstones of God’s creation.

And today, that often includes climate change. According to a 2025 survey from Pew Research Center, highly-religious Americans are more likely to believe God gave humans the duty to protect Earth, even in comparison to those who are moderately religious. However, there is also a history of cremation being a contentious issue in Catholicism, though the strictness has relaxed in recent years. Taboos about burial did not stop Sharon, and perhaps won’t stop others who don’t take the resurrection of the body literally. To many people, even those who are Christians, the body is the vessel for what really makes human beings special.

Your reaction to the details above might be a good litmus test for how you feel about human composting. But if you think it sounds disgusting, and to even think about it is macabre—that’s valid! The vast majority of Americans are still choosing traditional burial or cremation. Today, human composting is legal in more than a dozen states, with legislation in the process in several more.

#6244. 65 Years of Human Spaceflight at NASA Johnson

For 65 years, NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston has helped shape human spaceflight, from the Gemini missions that demonstrated rendezvous and docking techniques needed for Apollo to the research conducted aboard the International Space Station, which has supported a continuous human presence for more than 26 years. Today, Johnson teams are preparing crews and systems for NASA’s next chapter: returning astronauts to the lunar surface and building the capabilities needed for a long-term human presence at the Moon.

Across those missions, generations of flight controllers, engineers, scientists, instructors, medical specialists, and other experts have helped crews live and work beyond Earth. Johnson is home to NASA’s Orion and Moon Base programs, and its teams continue to support space station operations, astronaut training, spacecraft development, mission operations, and human health.

When the Manned Spacecraft Center officially opened on Nov. 1, 1961, NASA had already flown two suborbital Mercury missions, with the first orbital flight just months away. Most Project Mercury activities remained at Cape Canaveral in Florida to maintain continuity, but the new Project Gemini took up residence in Houston, housed in temporary leased facilities across the city while construction of the new Clear Lake campus continued. The new Mission Control Center became NASA’s primary flight control center in June 1965, with the Gemini IV mission that included the first American spacewalk. Houston became the nerve center for American human spaceflight, overseeing the remaining eight Gemini missions before transitioning to the Apollo program. Following the tragic Apollo 1 fire in January 1967, managers, engineers, and astronauts at the Manned Spacecraft Center applied lessons learned to make the spacecraft safer and ensure the safety of its astronauts, resuming crewed missions in October 1968.  Managers in Houston devised a daring plan to send Apollo 8 on a circumlunar flight.

In December 1968, Apollo 8 made its historic trip around the Moon, and seven months later Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong and Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin landed on the lunar surface. Their first voice transmission back to Earth after their arrival began with the word “Houston.”  Five more Moon landings completed the Apollo program and humanity’s first phase of lunar exploration in December 1972.

Following the Moon landings, scientists at the Manned Spacecraft Center’s Lunar Receiving Laboratory conducted initial analyses of Apollo lunar samples and prepared them for researchers around the world. After the building was demolished in March 2024, the Lunar Receiving Park was dedicated to honor the laboratory’s history in 2026. Today, Johnson’s Astromaterials Research and Exploration Science (ARES) division continues to analyze and curate the Apollo collection at the Lunar Sample Laboratory Facility.

Skylab, America’s first space station, ran into trouble during its launch in May 1973, losing its thermal shield, jamming one solar array and losing the other one.  In less than 10 days, engineers in Houston designed and built a sun shield and generated procedures to free the jammed array, followed by the first extensive in-orbit repair activities by the first Skylab crew. The three missions lasting 28, 59, and 84 days accomplished more research than planned, demonstrated the value of humans on long-duration missions, and provided operators in mission control with round-the-clock experience monitoring long duration human spaceflights.

In July 1975, after several joint training sessions in Houston and Moscow, American astronauts and Soviet cosmonauts met in space for the first time during the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project. Approved as a project in 1972, five approach and landing tests of the space shuttle using orbiter Enterprise paved the way for the first orbital mission of Columbia in 1981.

Engineers in Houston began designs for a reuseable space plane in the late 1960s, with the space shuttle receiving formal approval in 1972. During the 1970s, Johnson Space Center put in place the training and simulation facilities that astronauts used for the life of the program. Upgrades to mission control enabled the use of the latest technologies to support ever more complex space shuttle missions. The April 1981 launch of space shuttle Columbia inaugurated a new era of reusable spacecraft. The program’s 135 missions flew 355 individuals from 16 nations. Missions included satellite deployments and retrievals, dedicated Department of Defense flights, a variety of science missions including deployment of planetary spacecraft, ferrying crews and cargo to two different space stations, and doing the heavy lifting in the assembly of the orbiting laboratory. The program recovered from the tragic losses of the Challenger and Columbia crews with renewed emphasis on crew safety. The final space shuttle mission, STS-135, closed out the 30-year program in July 2011.

An Earth orbiting space station, first approved by President Ronald Reagan in 1984, underwent many modifications before taking on its current form as the International Space Station in 1993. Overall management of the program resides at Johnson. The first element launch took place in November 1998, followed one month later by the first U.S. element, the Node 1 Unity module. The first expedition crew took up residence on Nov. 2, 2000, and for more than 26 years, rotating crews of astronauts and cosmonauts have lived and worked aboard the orbiting laboratory, establishing a permanent human presence in low Earth orbit.

To date, 298 individuals from 26 countries have visited the space station, conducting more than 4,000 science experiments and educational activities to enable exploration missions and improve life on Earth.

Life aboard the space station depends on a global team on the ground. Crews conduct research and maintain equipment in microgravity, while Johnson teams at the Mission Control Center coordinate the agency’s station operations with international partners. Johnson’s Space Vehicle Mockup Facility supports training for NASA astronauts and international crews on station systems, science operations, and emergency procedures. At the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory, crews rehearse spacewalks around full-scale station mockups in one of the world’s largest indoor pools. Johnson’s Human Research Program also supports health investigations aboard the station, helping researchers understand how spaceflight affects the body so crews can thrive on future deep space missions.

What began as a framework of modules has evolved into a springboard for international cooperation, advanced scientific research and technology demonstrations, the development of a low Earth orbit economy, and NASA’s next giant leaps in exploration. The space station continues to be a proving ground for NASA’s Artemis program and human exploration of Mars.

The Artemis II mission marked the first crewed flight of NASA’s Orion spacecraft. The four-person crew launched April 1, on a nearly 10-day trip around the Moon. At its farthest point, Orion traveled 252,756 miles from Earth, farther than any humans had traveled before. The mission demonstrated Orion’s capabilities with astronauts aboard and tested crew operations in deep space, setting the stage for future lunar missions.

Building on Artemis II, NASA’s Artemis III mission will test integrated operations in low Earth orbit between Orion and test versions of one or both commercial human landing systems under development by SpaceX and Blue Origin. Astronauts will demonstrate the rendezvous and docking capabilities needed to transfer crews between spacecraft for the lunar landing planned for Artemis IV.

NASA’s Moon Base Program is planning a phased effort to support a sustained human presence near the Moon’s South Pole. The first phase will focus on robotic exploration, technology demonstrations, and preparations for future surface operations. Later phases will add infrastructure to support astronauts living and working on the Moon. Lunar terrain vehicles will help crews explore farther, transport equipment, and conduct science.

At Johnson, teams are drawing on decades of experience in astronaut training, mission control, spacecraft development, and human health to prepare for these missions. From training crews for lunar operations to developing the systems that will support them, Johnson is building on 65 years of human spaceflight experience for humanity’s return to the lunar surface through the Artemis and Moon Base Programs.

NASA explores the unknown in air and space, innovates for the benefit of humanity, and inspires the world through discovery.

#6243. Don’t Visit Ko Lipe

After 19 years, I finally went back to Ko Lipe, the Thai island I spent close to a month on in 2006. Back then, it was one of those super off-the-beaten-path destinations that few but the most intrepid travelers visited, where electricity only ran a few hours a day, basic bungalows right on the beach cost something like $2 USD, and there really was a last boat for the season.

There was much to do here but that was the point. You hung out on the beach, read a book, went snorkeling, went back to the beach, drank beers at the one beach bar on the island, rotated meals between the five restaurants there, and went to bed early.

It was paradise – and a place a lot of people got stuck. Days easily turned into weeks here.

If you asked me what the highlight of all my travels was, I would be the time I spent on Ko Lipe. I made incredible friends, lounged around, got to know the locals, learned a bit of Thai, and, overall, lived that idyllic backpacker life we all dream about.

Over the years, I’ve avoided going back to Ko Lipe because the memory of my time there is so strong that I didn’t want to ruin it. Any re-visit would simply be trying to recreated a magic that couldn’t be recreated because the people that it special wouldn’t be there. I’d be chasing travel ghosts. And, since I know my sleepy paradise has been developed greatly over the years, I was also too afraid seeing that would make me sad.

Tourism in Thailand tends toward the unsustainable. No island really develops in a good way. It’s all build, build, build.

And I didn’t want to see my Ko Lipe like that.

But as I was planning my recent trip through Southeast Asia, returning to Ko Lipe made sense. I was heading down the Indian Ocean side of Thailand on my way into Malaysia and I’d pass by it.

And, since I was looking for a lively place for New Year’s Eve, it seemed liked the best choice. I knew there would be travelers there and there were no other nearby islands that would work, especially since Ko Lipe has a boat to Langkawi, which was my next stop.

And I’m sad to report that Ko Lipe took the Ko Phi Phi model of tourism and is now extremely overdeveloped.

Most of the island is now paved over, the old dirt footpaths having become concrete for the cars and construction trucks. Swaths of palm trees are now the sites of high-end resorts with pools (on an island with no natural water supply). Construction of more resorts continues at a fast pace. The coral around the island is dying, a victim of all the boats, anchors, pollution, and overfishing. Beaches are now lined with boats, their exhaust spilling into the ocean, leaving a shiny film you can see as you swim. And the restaurants cater to tourists looking for bad Western food, not great Thai cuisine.

The island’s boom has displaced many locals, who were forced to sell to mainland developers, and much of the island’s workforce is now from the mainland. They see little of the benefits this tourism boom.

So lies Ko Lipe, another victim of Thailand’s all too common overdevelopment and exploitation of limited resources.

I met lots of people there who loved the island. If it’s your first time, I can see why you would love it. After all, the area is postcard perfect, the water is perfectly an azure blue, the sand is a beautiful white, and since you’re surrounded by a national park, a lot of tours take you to some secluded islands.

And, in comparison to Ko Phi Phi, Krabi, or Phuket, it is less developed so I can’t fault someone stepping here for the first time going “wow!”

But, as I reflect on the island and its overdevelopment, I have come to the same conclusion I have about Ko Phi Phi: people shouldn’t visit.

I’m not against growth, but I’m against this kind of growth. It’s not sustainably managed and going there will only tax the island’s limited resources even further. You can’t put the genie back in the bottle and no local is going to say “sure, I’ll stay broke so you can an idealized vision of the world.”

And, with so many other islands to visit that are well managed (Ko Lanta, Ko Jum, and Ko Mook, to name three nearby), I think you should skip Ko Lipe.

A visit there will only make things worse.

It pains me to say that, because it was such a beautiful place, and my original visit had a huge impact on my life. But if we’re going to be good stewards and travelers, sometimes you just have to say enough is enough.

And Ko Lipe is a place where enough is enough.

Go somewhere else that is better managed.

Riding elephants in Thailand went away when consumers became more conscious of it. Eco lodges got big because of consumers. Overtourism is talked about by consumers as much as it is by locals.

Maybe if enough people start to do something, Ko Lipe will change.

But, at the very least, by not going you are at least no contributing to the problem.

#6242. This week: Permitting bill hits Senate floor amid aviation funding fight

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally launched a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

The lame-duck session continues as lawmakers look ahead to Thanksgiving and the funding deadline that arrives in December. The primary legislative business this week is the Senate's bipartisan permitting overhaul, but a late-breaking aviation funding fight and the Senate Democratic leadership contest are also commanding attention.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally launched a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., and both men are accumulating supporters ahead of leadership votes that are currently scheduled for early December — though there's been an effort to move that up to this week.

Van Hollen has expressed disagreement with Schumer's participation in primaries.

​"I don't think it's the role of the Senate majority leader to get involved in open, contested Democratic primaries," Van Hollen said Sunday on CNN.

​Van Hollen has also said he wants to use all available tools to stop funding for the Iran war immediately, with a government funding deadline in December. That's going to be one of several flash points for December's funding discussions, as President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans try to use what leverage they have before Democrats take the gavels in the House and the Senate in January.

A new issue is the state of federal air traffic control after Friday's nationwide ground stop, with the Trump administration now seeking $50 billion to upgrade systems.

"I need additional money to do the additional work to keep the airspace safe," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Fox News Sunday.

Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, a senior appropriator who is in line to become majority whip, has suggested reallocating funds from the additional money the Trump administration and congressional Republicans allocated to Immigration and Customs Enforcement to address the challenges at the Federal Aviation Administration.

"There is a pot of 60 billion extra dollars on top of the regularly appropriated amount for ICE and we should use at least a portion of that money for the FAA. We can solve this problem and not spend any additional taxpayer dollars," Schatz posted on X.

"We can do all things, we don't have to do one versus the other," Duffy said in the Fox News Sunday interview. "I don't think that is the answer. The answer is let's do everything that's going to keep Americans safe, whether it's with immigration or it's with air travel."

Meanwhile on the Senate floor, the energy permitting overhaul bill faces a key test Monday evening​, with a vote scheduled to limit debate on a substitute amendment that represents the most recent version of the bill. Votes on a number of President Donald Trump's judicial nominations are also lined up this week.

On the other side of the Capitol, the House floor schedule i​ncludes several labor-related bills. ​One of the measures, introduced by Sen.-elect Kevin Hern, R-Okla.,​ would set standards for the way labor law applies to franchise operators.

New member orientation is also continuing, and committees in both the House and Senate will be holding hearings throughout the week as the outgoing Republican committee chairs aim to get through priority items on their agenda before the end of the Congress.

That includes a Tuesday morning Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing for Hung Cao, the nominee to be Navy secretary, who is currently the acting secretary. The Senate Judiciary Committee will be busy as well, as Chairman Charles E. Grassley, R-Iowa, looks to tee up more of Trump's judicial nominations for floor consideration.

#6241. Why This Company is One of the Best for Finding Work

Most travel is extractive and passive. You show up somewhere, take photos of the same landmarks everyone else takes photos of, eat at a restaurant the guidebook recommended, and hit up some bars. You take some tours to learn about the place and, if you’re lucky, get to meet some locals on your trip. You don’t really go deep.

Even long-term travelers who talk about how they “aren’t tourists” do the same – just at a slower pace and while trying to spend less money.

And there’s nothing wrong with that. That’s just the nature of travel. While we all imagine dropping into a place, befriending locals, and having this crazy time like we’re in some movies. But that doesn’t happen. Because we’re just passing through and, for the most part, locals don’t want to become friends with tourists. In fact, most locals don’t interact with tourists. (I mean it does happen but it’s not the norm.)

If you really want a deep travel experience, you need to stay. If you want to understand a place, you need to stay. The most transformative travel experiences I’ve ever had involved contributing something and staying somewhere long enough to build real relationships. It was being embedded in a place rather than just passing through.

I think that more travelers should give back when they travel. In the old days, it was hard to find out what organizations and opportunities were legit, vetted, and actually made the lives of locals better.

Now, there’s a ton of companies that can help you not only find meaningful volunteer jobs when you travel but also paid jobs when you travel and one of the best ones is Global Work & Travel. Use code NOMADICMATT to unlock a discount on your next trip.

Global Work & Travel is the world’s largest gap year company and has been placing people on working holidays, volunteer programs, teaching positions, internships, and more for nearly 2 decades. They’ve helped over 116,000 people and they cover destinations across, the UK and Europe, the Americas, Asia, Africa, and the Pacific.

Even for experienced travelers, moving abroad can be difficult. Finding employment as a traveler, securing permanent accommodation or getting stuck in shared rooms for months on end, transport costs in a new city, interview after interview competing against locals… This is just the beginning of what long term travelers need to consider.

Fortunately, companies like Global Work & Travel provide the scaffolding or safety net that makes working abroad possible for people who don’t want to figure everything out themselves. They handle job matching, pre-departure support, visa guidance, placement, and ongoing assistance through their gWorld portal, a personal trip management app that keeps everything organized in one place. For first-timers especially, having that support structure can be the difference between actually going and endlessly deliberating. The programs they offer span a wide range:

For the past decade, “digital nomad” has been the aspirational version of long term travel. Work remotely, earn in a strong currency, live somewhere cheaper, repeat.

But that model only really works for a small subset of people. You need a remote job, a certain income level, and often a level of career stability that most younger travelers simply don’t have yet.

Instead of bringing a job with you, you get one when you arrive. You integrate into the local economy instead of floating above it. You meet people through work, not just coworking spaces or short-term hostels. And you build a life somewhere, not just a temporary routine.

In a lot of ways, working holiday makers are having a more grounded and accessible version of what people think digital nomad life is. You’re not just passing through, you’re actually living there. You have coworkers, a schedule, a reason to stay longer than a week, and a chance to build real lifetime connections.

It’s also far more realistic for most people. You don’t need a remote business or years of experience. You just need the willingness to go and the right setup to make it happen.

That’s why I think we’re seeing a shift. Less “how do I work remotely?” and more “how do I actually live and work abroad for a year?”

And that’s exactly where structured programs like Global Work & Travel come in. They remove the biggest barriers, finding a job, navigating visas, getting set up, so people can actually make that shift from idea to reality.

For a lot of travelers, this isn’t just an alternative to digital nomad life. It’s a more sustainable, accessible, and realistic way to actually live and work abroad.

Volunteering abroad has a complicated reputation, and it’s worth being honest about that. There are lots of bad volunteer programs out there in the world. Programs that don’t really give back and are designed to make travelers “feel” like they did something but really are just profit driven campaigns. Global Work & Travel’s vets programs in the areas such as wildlife conservation, community development, education, and healthcare in the locations and countries it operates so you know the program you sign up for is legit.

The case for ethical, well-structured volunteering is genuinely strong. When you work alongside local Zanzibar communities on problems they’ve defined as priorities, or with wildlife and conservation in South Africa or Elephant rehabilitation in Thailand — something shifts in how you understand the world. Not only are you helping to give back to a place but you also understand the true needs of a the people and ecosystems living there, but also helping overcome the struggles they go through. It opens your mind and shifts your perspective.

Their Global Animal Welfare Fund also channels resources directly into conservation projects at their partner sites, so the impact extends beyond individual placements.

Working holidays let you truly experience a country instead of just visiting it. You immerse yourself in the culture by living like a local every day. You meet more people both locals and fellow travellers while building real friendships. Best of all, you get paid to travel, so you can stay much longer instead of rushing through in a few weeks. This lets you experience local life deeply, discover hidden spots, and understand how people really live in different places. You also build valuable skills, boost your resume with international experience, and make long-term travel more affordable since your income covers the costs. Plus, you gain a real cultural understanding that no short holiday can match. All that while stil getting paid? Not bad right?!

#6240. Laser Focus at the Top of the World

A next-generation geodetic instrument developed by NASA, part of a network that helps measure satellites’ orbits and the planet’s shape, has debuted in Svalbard, Norway.

More than 60 years ago, scientists at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center aimed a laser skyward and fired a pulse of light at an orbiting satellite equipped with special reflectors. By measuring the time it took for the light to return, they demonstrated a new, more precise method for tracking satellites.

Since then, satellite laser ranging (SLR) has grown more precise and more widely used. The technique now underpins many aspects of Earth observation, such as validating satellite orbits and mapping subtle changes to Earth’s surface. Pioneered at the Goddard Optical Research Facility—now the Goddard Geophysical and Astronomical Observatory—laser ranging is performed at more than 40 stations worldwide.

In 2026, the next generation of SLR, developed by NASA scientists and tested at Goddard, began to come online. On October 12, a faster, even more precise SLR system officially debuted at the Ny-Ålesund Geodetic Observatory in Svalbard, Norway, operated by the Norwegian Mapping Authority, a NASA partner. The observatory’s remote location in the Arctic archipelago is shown in this image, acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 in July 2026. It is the first NASA next-generation SLR system in operation and the northernmost SLR facility on Earth.

While the systems developed decades ago have been “workhorses” of the global laser tracking network, their age and the growing number of satellites have necessitated updates, said Stephen Merkowitz, project manager for NASA’s Space Geodesy Project. “We wanted newer systems that could track more objects, and track them more accurately and precisely,” he said.

Years of development, testing, and careful calibration produced the Space Geodesy Satellite Laser Ranging system now running at Ny-Ålesund. Among its features are lasers that can fire pulses thousands of times per second, up from tens of times per second, and sensors that can detect single photons, meaning that less light needs to be reflected back from a satellite.

Along with determining the orbits of satellites, SLR is critical for establishing the terrestrial reference frame, the foundation of modern coordinate systems and a common standard that allows measurements to be compared with one another. “If you want to know where your satellite observation is on a map, you need to have it in the proper reference frame,” Merkowitz said. In addition, tracking Earth’s center of mass, measuring changes in sea level and ice mass, studying the motion of tectonic plates, and maintaining global navigation satellite systems such as GPS, all rely on an accurate reference frame.

The far-north location of the Ny-Ålesund facility improves the distribution of SLR stations across the planet, making the whole network more robust. The location also allows the system to gather more data about polar-orbiting satellites, which include ICESat-2, GRACE-FO, and other Earth observation satellites. “From the station at Goddard [in Greenbelt, Maryland], we’ll catch the polar-orbiting satellites maybe two or three times a day,” Merkowitz said. “But from Ny-Ålesund, you’ll see them almost every orbit.”

Certain satellite missions may especially benefit from the Arctic location, he added. Take ICESat-2, designed to make precise observations of ice surface heights. Having a station tracking the satellite from an icy polar region could lead to more accurate measurements there. “When it’s over the ice, we want the calibration to be as good as possible,” Merkowitz said.

Innovations and lessons learned from the Svalbard installation will carry over to future ones, Merkowitz said. In particular, the Ny-Ålesund facility drove improvements in automation because the site is located next to a bird sanctuary. Access restrictions require the station to be remotely operated at certain times, such as during the summer breeding season for migratory birds. These capabilities can be refined and applied at other stations. NASA is currently building two more next-generation SLR systems to replace legacy instruments at Goddard and the McDonald Geodetic Observatory in Texas.

NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey. NASA photo by Julie Horvath (KBR). Story by Lindsey Doermann.

#6239. How the Antigravity 360 Drone Will Change Your Travels

Drones are huge. And, while there’s lots of restrictions around them, a lot of travelers take them on road because they produce some amazing sweeping aerial shots.

There’s lots of amazing brands out there but one that I think is super cool is the Antigravity A1. Released in late 2025, attempts to render the traditional gimbal obsolete for a vast segment of creators. By leveraging a dual-lens 360-degree capture system, the A1 records everything in every direction simultaneously. The result is a “fly now, frame later” experience that feels less like piloting a drone and more like directing a virtual camera in a pre-recorded digital environment.

I was sent one to use and want to share my experience and why I like this product so much.

What make’s Antigravity 360’s so special is the two lenses. Most drones feature a single lens that points forward. However, the A1 features two ultra-wide-angle lenses positioned on the top and bottom of the central fuselage that each captures a 200-degree field of view. When those images are combines, they overlap to create a seamless 360-degree sphere.

And, in the final exported footage, the drone itself is digitally removed, creating the illusion of a camera floating in mid-air with no visible means of support.

The sensors themselves are 1/1.28-inch CMOS units. While smaller than the 1-inch sensors found on some “Pro” level photography drones, they are massive compared to typical 360 action cameras. This allows for significantly better low-light performance and a higher dynamic range, capturing details in the highlights and shadows that would typically be lost in the harsh contrast of a midday sun.

Most countries require drones weighing 250 grams or more to be registered and subject to stricter flight rules. Antigravity clearly understood the importance of this threshold because they made the A1 to weigh exactly 249 grams with its standard battery meaning it’s not considered a commercial drone so you don’t have to register it.

And the drone feels remarkably sturdy. It utilizes a high-grade carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer that offers a better strength-to-weight ratio than the standard ABS plastic found in cheaper models. The folding mechanism is satisfyingly tactile, clicking into place with a precision that suggests long-term durability. When folded, the drone is roughly the size of a large smartphone, though about three times as thick.

The Vision Goggles: These are sleek, lightweight, and feature dual 4K micro-OLED displays with a 120Hz refresh rate. The latency is nearly non-existent and they have integrated head tracking. Because the drone is recording in 360 degrees, you aren’t limited to seeing what is in front of the drone. When you turn your head to the left, the goggle feed pans to the left. If you look down, you see the ground passing beneath you. This provides a sense of presence and spatial awareness that is simply impossible with a traditional fixed-camera drone.

The drone uses a single-handed motion controller. You point the controller where you want to go and pull the trigger to accelerate. Tilt your wrist left to bank, or raise the nose of the controller to climb. It is an incredibly intuitive system that allows even a novice to fly through complex environments within minutes. For professional FPV pilots who prefer the precision of manual acrobatic flight, the A1 does support a traditional “Mode 2” stick controller, but the motion controls are so fluid that most users will likely never switch back.

The marketing for the Antigravity 360 proudly displays “8K Resolution.” In a traditional camera, 8K means every pixel is packed into a 16:9 rectangle. In 360 video, those pixels are spread across a full sphere. When you “reframe” that 8K sphere into a standard flat video, you are looking at a “crop” of the total image.

The color science is noticeably improved over previous 360 cameras. The A1 features a “Vivid” profile for those who want punchy, social-media-ready colors, and a 10-bit “Log” profile for professional editors who need to match the footage to other cameras in a color-grading suite. The stabilization, powered by Antigravity’s “FlowState” algorithms, is nothing short of miraculous. You can fly in 20mph winds, and the footage remains as steady as if the camera were on a tripod.

The “Antigravity Studio” app allows you to download footage wirelessly (at speeds up to 80MB/s) and reframe your video using your phone’s gyroscope. You simply watch the video and move your phone around to “film” the scene in real-time. The app also features “Auto-Frame,” an AI tool that identifies subjects and automatically generates a cut that keeps them in focus. For a solo creator, this effectively provides a virtual camera crew that never misses a shot.

Battery technology remains the bottleneck for all small drones. The A1’s standard Intelligent Flight Battery provides a theoretical 24 minutes of flight. In real-world conditions with moderate wind and constant recording, expect closer to 19 or 20 minutes.

While 20 minutes sounds short, the “work per minute” is much higher than a traditional drone. Because you don’t need to re-fly a path to get different angles, a single 20-minute flight can yield the same amount of usable footage as three flights with a Mavic. For those who need more time, the “Pro Battery” (which pushes the weight over 250g) offers a staggering 39 minutes of flight time, though it does compromise the drone’s agility slightly.

In terms of flight dynamics, the A1 is a “cinewhoop” style flyer. It is stable and predictable rather than aggressive and twitchy. It has a top speed of roughly 36 mph, which is plenty for following bikes or cars, but it won’t keep up with a professional racing drone. The “Turtle Mode” is a life-saver; if you crash and end up upside down, the drone can flip itself over using its propellers, allowing you to take off again without a “walk of shame” to recover the aircraft.

The Antigravity 360 is a niche product that is rapidly becoming mainstream.

The Antigravity 360 (A1) is the most exciting drone I have tested. By removing the need for a gimbal and the stress of manual framing, it allows the pilot to focus on the one thing that truly matters: the story they are trying to tell.

While the image quality isn’t quite at the level of a high-end cinema drone, and the lenses are admittedly delicate, these are small prices to pay for the creative liberation the A1 provides. It bridges the gap between traditional cinematography and the immersive world of VR.

If you are a creator who is tired of the same old “drone shots” and want to push the boundaries of what is possible in the air, the Antigravity 360 is an essential addition to your toolkit.

Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.

Explanation: If you stare into space for a long time, what might you see? At first, you might only see the usual brightest stars, but if your eyes (or camera) could continue to collect light, you would see increasingly more. In the direction of the featured image, after only a few minutes, you would begin to notice some regions without stars. As your staring continued, the dark region would become better defined, and after a full 20 hours, you would notice a strange dark structure. To celebrate, you use digital processing to brighten the image and enhance the colors. At the end, you might have an excellent image of Lynds 1251 (LDN 1251), a star-forming region laced with opaque brown-appearing interstellar dust.
